areas.name: Around the house
areas.blurb: Everyday home fixes and safety checks for power, water, air, alarms, and walls, plus the science behind them.
areas.intro: These guides cover the small jobs and safety checks that keep a home running: resetting power, shutting off water, fixing a running toilet, clearing clogs, changing the furnace filter, testing alarms, and simple wall repairs. Each one also explains the science or math behind the job, from watts and amps to water pressure and buoyancy. The electrical guides stick to what homeowners commonly do safely, like resetting and testing; anything involving wiring belongs to a licensed electrician.

deeper.label: The Trades
deeper.text: Ready for more? Full courses on plumbing, electrical, HVAC and construction: how every part of a house works, how the parts fit together, how to troubleshoot by symptom, and which jobs to leave to licensed pros.

areas.name: Car basics
areas.blurb: Everyday car checks and roadside fixes, plus the science that makes them work.
areas.intro: These guides cover the checks and small fixes that keep a car safe and running: oil, tires, fluids, wipers, warning lights, a flat tire, and a dead battery. Each one also explains the science under the hood, from gas laws to levers to the chemistry of antifreeze. For anything specific to your car, your owner's manual is always the final word.

deeper.label: Cars: How They Work and How to Fix Them
deeper.text: Ready for more? A free 14-lesson course on how every system works, how the parts fit together, how to troubleshoot by symptom, and which jobs to do yourself.

areas.name: Money and taxes
areas.blurb: Paychecks, budgets, bank accounts, interest, credit, taxes, scams, and insurance, with the math behind each one.
areas.intro: Money skills are life skills, and most of them come down to a little math and a few good habits. These guides cover reading a paycheck, budgeting, banking, interest, credit, filing taxes, spotting scams, and insurance. They follow U.S. rules and official sources like the IRS, CFPB, FTC, and FDIC. They teach how money works and are not personal financial advice.

areas.name: Kitchen and everyday life
areas.blurb: Cook and store food safely, do laundry, and take the first big grown-up steps: renting, job hunting and voting.
areas.intro: These guides cover skills you'll use almost every day once you live on your own. The kitchen guides follow U.S. food safety advice from USDA, FDA and CDC. The later guides cover renting, applying for a job and registering to vote, using U.S. rules that often differ from state to state.

guides.name: Reset a Tripped Circuit Breaker
guides.time: about 10 minutes (about an hour to label a whole panel)
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 7, help from about 10, do it alone from about 13.
guides.intro: When part of your home suddenly loses power, a circuit breaker has often switched itself off to protect the wiring. Knowing where your breaker panel is, how to reset a breaker, and which breaker runs which room saves time in the dark. This guide is for U.S.-style breaker panels and covers only the switches a homeowner is meant to use.
need: Flashlight
Pen and paper, or the label card inside the panel door
Masking tape (optional, for labels)
A helper (for labeling the panel)
before: If you see sparks, hear sizzling or buzzing, or smell something burning, don't go near the panel. Call the fire department right away.
If the panel is wet, or you can see any wires, don't touch it. Call a licensed electrician.
Turn off the lights and unplug appliances in the rooms that lost power.

steps.how: Walk around and note which lights and outlets stopped working. Turn off the light switches and unplug appliances in those rooms, so nothing switches on the moment power comes back.
In many homes, especially older ones, the panel is in a garage or a storage closet. Some homes have more than one panel, inside or outside.
Open the panel door. Breakers are rows of small switches. A tripped one sits all the way at OFF or stuck partway between ON and OFF.
Stand a little to the side of the panel. Using one hand, push the tripped handle firmly all the way to OFF.
Now push the handle firmly to ON. Close the panel door.
See if the lights and outlets work again. Plug things back in one at a time, and spread big power users across different circuits instead of running them all on one.
If the breaker trips again right away, or you can't figure out why it tripped, leave it OFF and call a licensed electrician.

On a calm day, with a helper, switch off one breaker at a time and note which lights and outlets go dark. Write the rooms on the panel's label card. Warn everyone first, since clocks and computers will lose power.
Show everyone in the household where the panel is and what a tripped breaker looks like.

guides.pro: Call a licensed electrician if a breaker trips again right after you reset it or keeps tripping. Call an electrician instead of resetting if the panel is wet, you can see wires, or more than one breaker has tripped. Call a licensed electrician soon if lights dim or flicker, or if outlets, switches, plugs, or cords feel unusually warm. If you see sparks, hear sizzling or buzzing, or smell something burning, call the fire department right away.
guides.how_it_works: Why a breaker trips — Electric current is the flow of electric charge through a wire, measured in amps. Voltage is the push that moves the current, measured in volts. In standard U.S. homes, regular outlets supply 120 volts. — Power, measured in watts, tells how fast a device uses energy. You find it by multiplying volts by amps. Each breaker protects one circuit and allows only a set number of amps. If more current flows than that, the wires could get too hot, so the breaker switches itself off. That's called tripping. — Here is the math for a 15-amp circuit: 120 volts × 15 amps = 1,800 watts. Say your space heater's label says 1,500 watts and your microwave's label says 1,000 watts. Together that's 2,500 watts. Divide by 120 volts and you get about 21 amps, which is more than 15. Click: the breaker trips.
guides.teach: Visit the panel together in daylight, long before you ever need it. Let your child hold the flashlight and find the tripped switch while you reset it. Make labeling a team project: one person flips breakers, the other walks around and reports what went dark. Turn appliance labels into a math game with the watts formula.
mistakes: Resetting the same breaker over and over. — A breaker that keeps tripping is a warning sign. Leave it off and call a licensed electrician.
Pushing a tripped handle straight to ON, and nothing happens. — Push it firmly all the way to OFF first, then to ON.
Running a space heater and a microwave on the same circuit. — Spread high-wattage appliances across different circuits.
A panel with no labels, so you guess in the dark. — Map and label every breaker now, while the power is on and nothing is wrong.
safety: Never touch a panel that is wet. Call an electrician.
If you can see any wires in the panel, stop and call an electrician.
Use extension cords and power strips only for temporary needs.
tips: Keep a flashlight near the panel.
Write down each time a breaker trips and what was running. A pattern helps an electrician find the cause.
Extension cords and power strips are for temporary use only.
Don't run a space heater on a light-duty extension cord. It can't carry that much current.

guides.name: Test and Reset a GFCI Outlet
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 6, help from about 8, do it alone from about 10.
guides.intro: A GFCI (ground-fault circuit interrupter) outlet is the kind with TEST and RESET buttons, usually found near water in kitchens, bathrooms, garages, and outdoors. It cuts the power in a split second when electricity starts leaking where it shouldn't, such as through water or a person. Testing it once a month tells you it still works, and knowing how to reset it can bring a 'dead' outlet back to life.
need: A small lamp or night-light that you know works
Paper and pencil (to note which outlets each GFCI controls)
before: If the GFCI has tripped, unplug whatever was running on it and check the cord for fraying or other damage.

steps.how: Look for outlets with TEST and RESET buttons in bathrooms, the kitchen, the garage, the basement or crawl space, laundry and utility sinks, and outdoors. Some homes have GFCI breakers in the panel instead, with a TEST button on the breaker.
Plug a lamp or night-light into the GFCI outlet and turn it on. If it doesn't light, press RESET first.
Push the TEST button. The light should go out. On a GFCI breaker, pressing TEST should move the handle to the tripped position.
Push RESET firmly. The light should come back on. For a GFCI breaker, reset the handle.
A GFCI outlet also protects the outlets wired after it on the same circuit. Next time you test, check which other outlets lose power and write them down.
If a regular outlet stops working, look for a tripped GFCI on the same circuit, which may be in another room. Unplug what was running, then press RESET.
If the light stays on when you press TEST, or won't come back on after RESET, the GFCI is not doing its job. Have a qualified electrician fix or replace it.
Test each GFCI once a month and after a power outage.

guides.pro: If the light stays on when you press TEST, the GFCI isn't working or isn't installed right. Have a qualified electrician correct it. If RESET won't bring the power back, the GFCI needs to be replaced. Replacing it is wiring work, so have a qualified electrician do it. If a GFCI keeps tripping, or you can't tell why it tripped, contact an electrician.
guides.how_it_works: How a GFCI notices a leak — Electricity travels in a loop. Current flows out to your lamp on one wire and comes back on another. In a healthy circuit, the amount going out equals the amount coming back. — A GFCI keeps comparing those two amounts. If some current is missing on the way back, it must be leaking out another path, maybe through water or a person. When the difference reaches just a few thousandths of an amp, about 4 to 6 milliamps, the GFCI shuts off the power in less than a tenth of a second. — A milliamp is one-thousandth of an amp. That means a GFCI can notice a leak far smaller than the current a lamp uses, and act on it faster than you can blink.
guides.teach: Make testing a first-of-the-month family routine. Let your child press TEST and RESET while you both watch the lamp. Draw a simple house map together showing which outlets go dark when each GFCI trips.
mistakes: Deciding an outlet is broken when it's really fed by a tripped GFCI somewhere else. — Check the GFCI outlets in nearby bathrooms, the kitchen, garage, basement, and outside, and press RESET.

Never testing because the outlet 'works fine'. — A GFCI can stop protecting you and still deliver power. In one CPSC survey, about a quarter of people who tested their GFCIs found one that wasn't working. Test monthly.
Pressing RESET over and over on a GFCI that keeps tripping. — Unplug everything on it. If it still trips, or you can't tell why, call an electrician.
safety: Test GFCIs once a month.
If TEST doesn't cut the power, don't count on that outlet for protection until a qualified electrician fixes it.
tips: Use a lamp you can see from the outlet so you know right away when it goes off.
Test after every power outage too.
If a GFCI trips every time one certain appliance is plugged in, that appliance may be faulty. Stop using it.
For outdoor power tools and electric garden equipment, use portable GFCI protection.

guides.name: Shut Off Your Home's Water
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 6, help from about 9, do it alone from about 12.
guides.intro: When a pipe bursts or a sink overflows, every minute of running water adds to the damage. Your home has a main shutoff valve that stops water to the whole house, and most sinks and toilets have their own small valves. Find them now, before you need them.
need: Flashlight
A tag or tape and a marker, for labeling
A water key or wrench, only if your main valve needs one
before: Learn where the main valve is now, before there's a leak.
Leave the valve at the water meter or property line alone. For that one, call your water utility or a licensed plumber.

steps.t: Look where the water comes in
steps.how: The main valve is usually close to where the water line enters the house. In a basement, check the front wall facing the street, typically within 3 to 5 feet of where the pipe comes in. In a home without a basement, look near the water heater or under the kitchen sink. Some are on an outside wall or in an underground box.
A round wheel handle closes by turning clockwise, and it may take two or more full turns. A lever handle closes with a quarter turn; it's off when the lever sits crossways to the pipe.
Turn the handle to closed with steady pressure. If it's rusted, stuck, or won't close all the way, plan to have a licensed plumber repair or replace it.
Open a faucet on the highest floor. This lets out the leftover pressure. The water should slow and stop. If it keeps flowing, the valve isn't closing fully.
Open a wheel valve about half a turn, or a lever about halfway, so the pipes fill gently. Then open it all the way and let each faucet run until the sputtering air stops.

Look under sinks and behind toilets for small valves on the water lines. A toilet's valve is usually on the wall behind it and closes clockwise. These let you shut off one fixture and keep water running everywhere else.
Tag the main valve so it's easy to spot. Show everyone in the family where it is and how to turn it.

guides.pro: If your home has no main valve, or it's rusted, stuck, or won't shut off completely, have a licensed plumber repair or replace it. For the valve at the meter or property line, call your water utility or a licensed plumber.
guides.how_it_works: Water pressure and the one way in — The water in your pipes is under pressure. Pressure is a force spread over an area, measured in pounds per square inch (psi). Many homeowners set their house pressure to around 50 psi. A widely used plumbing code calls for a pressure regulator, a valve that lowers the pressure, when the supply pressure is over 80 psi. — Where does the push come from? Water systems use pumps, and water stored up high in tanks. Each foot of water height adds about 0.433 psi at the bottom. So if the water's surface sits 115 feet above your faucet, it pushes with about 115 × 0.433, which is close to 50 psi. — That pressure fills every pipe in your house at once. But all of it comes in through one service line, and the main valve sits on that line. Close it, and no new water can get in. Open a faucet to let out the leftover pressure, and the flow stops everywhere downstream.
guides.teach: Go on a valve hunt together: the main valve first, then every sink and toilet. Let your child practice closing and opening a fixture valve while you watch. Play 'what would you do?': 'Water is spraying under the bathroom sink. What do you turn first?'
mistakes: Hunting for the valve while water pours in. — Find it and tag it today.
Turning a lever handle around and around like a wheel. — A lever only needs a quarter turn. It's off when it points across the pipe.
Opening the main valve all the way at once after a repair. — Open it partway, let the pipes fill, then open it fully and let the air out of the faucets.
Using the valve at the meter or curb. — Use your home's own main valve. Call the water utility or a licensed plumber for the one at the meter.
safety: Don't operate the valve at the meter or property line yourself. Call your water utility or a licensed plumber.
tips: If a pipe breaks or bursts, close the main valve right away. The faster the water is off, the less damage it can do.
Check the main valve now and then to make sure it isn't rusty and still closes completely.
If your home has fire sprinklers, there may be two valves. Unless a sprinkler pipe is the one leaking, close only the household plumbing valve and leave the sprinkler pipes on.
Keep a flashlight near the main valve.

guides.name: Fix a Running Toilet
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 7, help from about 9, do it alone from about 12.
guides.intro: A toilet that keeps running, or refills on its own, is quietly pouring water and money down the drain. A worn flapper alone can silently leak thousands of gallons a year. Most fixes happen inside the tank, with cheap parts and no special tools.
need: Food coloring or a toilet dye tablet
An old towel (to set the tank lid on)
Your phone, to photograph the old flapper
A replacement flapper that matches your toilet (if needed)
Rubber gloves (optional)
before: Before you replace any parts, close the toilet's shutoff valve by turning it clockwise, then flush to empty the tank.

steps.how: Lift off the tank lid and set it on a towel. Put a few drops of food coloring in the tank. Don't flush. Wait at least 10 minutes. If color shows up in the bowl, water is leaking past the flapper.
Flush right after the test so the dye doesn't stain the tank.
Watch the tank refill. If water keeps spilling into the tall open tube in the middle (the overflow tube), the water level is set too high.

The water should stop about 1/2 to 1 inch below the top of the overflow tube. For a ball on an arm, turn the adjusting screw where the arm meets the fill valve. For a float that slides on the fill valve, squeeze its clip and slide it down. Flush and check again.
The chain from the handle to the flapper should be neither too short nor too long. Too short, and it holds the flapper open; too long, and it can tangle or get caught under the flapper.
If you have to jiggle the handle to stop the running, tighten the nut that holds the handle to the tank. If that doesn't help, the handle may need replacing.

Turn off the water and flush to empty the tank. Unhook the old flapper and take it, or a photo of it, to the store to find a match. Hook on the new one, attach the chain about as it was, turn the water back on, and flush to test.
Repeat the dye test to make sure the leak is gone.

guides.pro: If the toilet keeps running or won't flush after these fixes, contact a local plumber.
guides.how_it_works: Floats, valves, and the siphon — The tank stores water for the next flush. When you push the handle, a lever lifts the flapper, and tank water rushes into the bowl. — The bowl drains through a curved pipe called the trapway. The rush of water fills it and pushes out the air, and that change in pressure starts a siphon. The siphon pulls water and waste down the drain until air gets back in and breaks it, which is the gurgle at the end of a flush. — As the tank empties, the float drops and opens the fill valve. Water pours in and the float rises with it. It floats because water pushes up on it with a force equal to the weight of the water it pushes aside. At the set level, the rising float shuts the valve. — If the flapper doesn't seal, water trickles into the bowl, the tank level slowly drops, and the fill valve turns on again by itself. That's why a worn flapper can make a toilet seem to flush or refill on its own.
guides.teach: Let your child do the dye test. It feels like a science experiment. Flush with the tank lid off so they can watch the flapper, chain, float, and fill valve move in order. Leak math: EPA says an average home's leaks can waste more than 9,300 gallons a year. Divide by 365 to find about how many gallons a day that is (about 25). Bring them along to the hardware store to match the flapper.
mistakes: Chain too tight, so the flapper never fully closes. — Leave a little slack so the chain rests without lifting the flapper.
Chain too long, so it gets caught under the flapper. — Hook it to a different link to shorten it.
Water level set too high, so water trickles down the overflow tube. — Lower the float until the water stops about 1/2 to 1 inch below the top of the tube.
Buying a flapper that doesn't match. — Take the old flapper or a photo to the store and match it.
tips: Do the dye test at least once a year.
EPA WaterSense suggests replacing the flapper at least every five years.
When buying a flapper, check its width and whether it has a foam float. Take the old one or a photo with you.
Mark the water line in the tank with a pencil before you adjust the float, so you can compare.

guides.name: Unclog a Sink or Toilet
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 6, help from about 9, do it alone from about 11.
guides.intro: Clogs happen in every home. A plunger clears most sink and toilet clogs in a few minutes, with no chemicals. Knowing which plunger to grab, how to get a good seal, and when to stop saves a mess and sometimes a service call.
need: Cup plunger (a plain rubber cup) for sinks, tubs, and showers
Flange plunger (a cup with an extra rubber sleeve) for toilets
Rubber gloves
Old towels or rags
A bucket
Hand drain snake (optional)
before: If the toilet bowl is full and not draining, don't flush again. It can overflow.
If someone has already poured a chemical drain cleaner into the drain, don't plunge it and don't add any other product. Call a plumber.

steps.how: Use a cup plunger for sinks, tubs, and showers. Use a flange plunger, with its extra rubber lip, for toilets. It seals better in the toilet's drain.
For a sink, stuff a wet rag into the overflow hole near the rim. For a double sink, plug the other drain. This keeps your push aimed at the clog.
You need enough water to cover the plunger's cup so it can seal. If a toilet bowl is very full, scoop some water into a bucket first.
Set the plunger over the drain so the cup covers the opening completely.
Press down smoothly, then pull up sharply. Repeat 20 to 30 times without breaking the seal. In a toilet, use quick, strong strokes.
Lift the plunger and watch. If the water drains, run water to rinse the sink. Flush a toilet only once its bowl drains normally. If it doesn't drain, try another round.
If plunging fails, a hand drain snake can reach farther. Feed the cable into the drain and crank the handle until you feel resistance. Turn it to hook or break up the clog, then pull it out.
If the clog still won't clear, call a plumber.

guides.pro: If plunging and a hand snake don't clear the clog, call a plumber. If water backs up in more than one place, like a toilet or shower when the washing machine drains, the blockage may be farther down the line. Call a plumber.
guides.how_it_works: Why a plunger works — Pressure is force spread over an area. When you push a plunger down, your force presses on the water trapped under the cup. — Water is very close to incompressible, which means it barely squeezes smaller. Instead of shrinking, it passes the push along. Pascal's principle says a change in pressure in one part of a fluid travels through all of it. So your push travels down the pipe to the clog. Pulling up sharply tugs the other way, rocking the clog back and forth until it breaks loose. — That's why the seal and the water matter. Air squeezes easily, so a cup full of air just squishes. And if the overflow hole is open, the push escapes out of it instead of reaching the clog.
guides.teach: Show your child the two plungers and let them pick the right one for each job. Practice on a slow sink first. It's less messy than a toilet. Talk about what never goes down a toilet: dental floss, hair, gum, and anything that isn't toilet paper. Keep a plunger near each toilet so no one has to hunt for one in a hurry.
mistakes: Flushing a clogged toilet again to 'push it through'. — Don't. If the water is high and not draining, another flush can overflow the bowl. Plunge instead.
Using a cup plunger on a toilet. — Use a flange plunger. Its rubber sleeve seals in the toilet's drain.
Plunging a sink with the overflow hole open. — Plug the overflow with a wet rag so the pressure goes toward the clog.
Mixing drain cleaners, or plunging after using one. — Never mix products, and never plunge a drain that has chemical cleaner in it. Call a plumber.
safety: Never mix drain cleaners or other cleaning products. They can react and give off dangerous fumes.
Don't use a plunger on a drain with chemical drain cleaner in it.
tips: Keep a cover or strainer over sink and tub drains to catch hair and food bits.
Never pour grease down a drain. Let it cool in a can, then put it in the trash.
Clean hair out of the tub drain after washing your hair.
Wear rubber gloves and lay an old towel around the base. It can get messy.

guides.name: Change a Furnace Air Filter
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 6, help from about 8, do it alone from about 11.
guides.intro: Most homes with central heating or air conditioning have an air filter that catches dust before air runs through the system. A clogged filter blocks airflow, wastes energy, and can let dirt reach parts that are hard to clean. Changing it is one of the easiest home jobs there is.
need: A new filter in the exact size printed on the old one
Marker
Flashlight
Screwdriver, if the filter cover has screws
Step stool or ladder, if the filter is up high or in the attic
before: Turn the heating and cooling system off at the thermostat.

steps.how: Go to the furnace or air handler, which may be in a utility room, basement, closet, attic, crawl space, or garage. The filter usually slides into a slot between the return duct and the unit. In some homes it sits behind a return-air grille in a wall or ceiling instead.
Switch the system off at the thermostat before you open anything.
Open the cover (it may have screws, clips, or a latch) and slide the filter out. Handle it carefully; the wire on some filters can be sharp.
The length, width, and thickness are printed on the cardboard frame. Buy that exact size. It should cover the opening and fit snugly without bending.
Look for the airflow arrow on the new filter's frame. Point it into the duct, toward the furnace, the way the air moves.
Take off the plastic wrap (not the cardboard frame) and write today's date where you'll see it next time.

steps.t: Slide it in and close up
steps.how: Slide the filter into the slot, arrow toward the furnace. Put the cover back on. Don't tape it shut, since you'll open it again.
Set the thermostat back to normal. Put a reminder on the calendar for the next check.

guides.pro: Before switching to a MERV 13 or higher filter, ask an HVAC technician or your service company whether your system can handle it.
guides.how_it_works: How a filter catches dust — A fan in the system pulls air from your rooms through the return duct, pushes it through the filter, heats or cools it, and sends it back out. The filter is a mat of fibers. Air slips through the gaps, while many particles, like dust and pollen, get caught. — MERV stands for Minimum Efficiency Reporting Value. It's a number for comparing filters: the higher the MERV, the better the filter is at trapping small particles. But a filter that catches more can also clog faster and slow the airflow, so your system has to be able to handle it. — As a filter fills up, air has a harder time getting through. That lowers the system's efficiency, and some dirty air can sneak around the filter onto the cooling coil. Energy.gov says replacing a dirty, clogged filter can cut an air conditioner's energy use by 5% to 15%. One more fact: a filter only cleans the air while the system is running.
guides.teach: Let your child read the size off the old filter and find the match at the store. Make the arrow rule a chant: 'Arrow points to the furnace.' Hold the old and new filters side by side so they can see what the filter caught. Let them write the date on the new filter.
mistakes: Putting the filter in backward. — Point the arrow into the duct, toward the furnace.
Buying a filter that's 'close enough' in size. — Match all three numbers on the frame. It should cover the opening and fit snugly without bending.
Forgetting when you last changed it. — Write the date on the frame and set a calendar reminder.
Jumping to the highest MERV without checking. — Ask an HVAC pro whether your system can handle it.
safety: Turn the system off at the thermostat before you pull the filter.
Handle filters carefully. The wire on some can be sharp.
Use a ladder if the filter is in the attic.
tips: How often depends on your filter and system, so follow the maker's directions. EPA says many makers suggest every 60 to 90 days. Energy.gov suggests every month or two during cooling season.
Check more often if you have pets, a dusty home, or the system runs constantly.
If the old filter looks very dirty when you change it, change it more often.
If your slot fits more than one thickness, the thicker filter has more surface area for catching dust.
Buy a few filters at a time so you always have a spare.

guides.name: Test Smoke and CO Alarms
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 5, help from about 8, do it alone from about 12.
guides.intro: Smoke alarms and carbon monoxide (CO) alarms are some of the cheapest life-savers in a home, but only if they work. Testing them takes a few minutes a month. Knowing their age, where they belong, and what to do when one sounds matters just as much.
need: A sturdy step stool or ladder
Replacement batteries of the type printed on each alarm
Marker and paper
A helper to steady the ladder
before: Read the instructions for each alarm. Mounting, testing, and replacement details can vary by model.

steps.how: Walk through the house and list each alarm. Smoke alarms belong inside each bedroom, outside each sleeping area, and on every level of the home, including the basement.
Push each smoke alarm's test button. It should sound loudly. Do this once a month.
If an alarm doesn't sound, put in a new battery and test again. If it still doesn't sound, replace the alarm.
Look on the back for the date it was made. Replace any smoke alarm that is 10 years old or older, even if it still beeps.
If your alarms use replaceable batteries, change them at least once a year. Sealed 10-year alarms don't get new batteries; you replace the whole alarm when its time is up.
Test CO alarms monthly. They belong outside sleeping areas and on every level of the home. Check the manual for when to replace them.
A chirp from a smoke alarm usually means its battery is low; replace the battery right away. A loud, steady alarm means danger.
If the CO alarm sounds, everyone goes outside to fresh air right away, then you call 911. Nobody goes back in until emergency responders say it's safe.

guides.pro: Hardwired alarms, the kind wired into the house, should be installed by a qualified electrician. If a CO alarm went off and you suspect an appliance, don't use that appliance again until trained service personnel have checked it.
guides.how_it_works: Two ways to sense smoke, and one gas you can't — Ionization alarms hold a tiny, safely shielded amount of radioactive material. It lets the air between two metal plates carry a small electric current. When smoke drifts in, the particles grab the charged bits of air and carry them away, so the current drops. When it drops enough, the alarm sounds. These respond faster to fast, flaming fires. — Photoelectric alarms shine a light beam through a dark chamber, aimed so it misses a light sensor. When smoke drifts in, the particles scatter the light, and some of it bounces onto the sensor. These respond faster to slow, smoldering fires. Because no one knows what kind of fire might start, safety agencies recommend having both kinds, or dual-sensor alarms. — Carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas with no color and no smell. Your nose can't warn you, so a CO alarm has to.
guides.teach: Let your child press the test button while a grown-up steadies the ladder, so they know the sound. Teach the difference: a chirp means 'change my battery'; a loud, steady alarm means 'get out'. Make a chart of every alarm, where it is, and its replace-by year. Practice the CO plan: outside first, then call 911.
mistakes: Pulling the battery because cooking keeps setting off the alarm. — Use the hush button, or move the alarm a few feet farther from the kitchen. Disabling an alarm can be a deadly mistake.
Keeping an old smoke alarm because it still beeps. — Replace smoke alarms 10 years from the date they were made.
Having alarms only in hallways. — Add one inside each bedroom too, and on every level.
Ignoring a CO alarm because nobody smells anything. — CO has no smell. Treat every CO alarm as real: go outside, then call 911.
safety: If the CO alarm sounds, move everyone outside to fresh air right away, then call 911.
Stay out until emergency responders say it's safe to go back in.
Never disable a smoke alarm or take out its battery.
Test smoke alarms every month.
tips: Pick an easy date for battery changes, like when you change your clocks.
Interconnected alarms are best: when one sounds, they all sound.
Mount smoke alarms on the ceiling or high on a wall, following the instructions. CPSC says wall alarms go about 6 to 12 inches below the ceiling.
If cooking sets off an alarm, open a window, press the hush button, or wave a towel. Never take out the battery.
A CO alarm's test button checks its circuits, not the accuracy of its sensor, so replace it on time.
There are alarms with strobe lights or vibration for people who are deaf or hard of hearing.

guides.name: Find a Stud and Hang a Picture
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 6, help from about 8, do it alone from about 12.
guides.intro: Hanging a picture well means it sits level and stays on the wall. Behind most walls are wooden posts called studs, and a hook or screw that reaches a stud holds much better than one in drywall alone. When there's no stud where you need one, a wall anchor rated for the weight does the job.
need: Stud finder
Tape measure
Pencil
Bubble level
Picture hook, eye-hook, or screw
Wall anchors rated for your picture's weight (if there's no stud)
Hammer, and a drill or screwdriver
Painter's tape (optional)
before: Pick a spot where a heavy frame or mirror won't hang over a bed, couch, or chair, in case it ever falls.

steps.how: Have a helper hold the picture up while you step back. Lightly mark the top center with a pencil.

Slide a stud finder sideways along the wall and mark where it signals. Mark the middle of the stud, not its edge. Studs run from floor to ceiling and are usually 16 or 24 inches apart, so once you find one, measure over to check for the next.
Try pushing a thumbtack into the wall. If it won't break the surface, the wall is probably plaster rather than drywall.
Pull the picture's wire up tight, the way it will hang, and measure from the wire to the top of the frame. Your hook goes that far below where you want the top of the frame.

steps.t: Use the stud if you can
steps.how: Use a hook or screw long enough to go through the drywall and into the stud. For large pictures, FEMA suggests eye-hooks at least 1 to 2 inches long. You should feel steady resistance the whole way in; if it suddenly goes easy, you've probably missed the stud.

steps.t: Use an anchor if there's no stud
steps.how: Pick an anchor whose package says it holds more than your picture weighs. Drill the hole size the package lists, tap the anchor in until it's flush, then drive in the screw.

steps.t: Use two hooks for big frames
steps.how: Large pictures and mirrors are steadier on two hooks than on one. Space them evenly from the center.
Hang the picture, set the bubble level on top of the frame, and nudge it until the bubble sits between the lines.

guides.how_it_works: Spacing, measuring, and the bubble — Studs are usually spaced 16 or 24 inches apart. Builders measure that spacing from the center of one stud to the center of the next, called 'on center.' If you find a stud center 30 inches from a corner and the spacing is 16 inches, the next ones are likely near 46 and 62 inches. The pattern helps you guess, and the stud finder confirms. — Hanging height is subtraction. If you want the top of the frame at 64 inches and the tight wire sits 4 inches below the top, the hook goes at 64 − 4 = 60 inches. To center a picture on a wall, divide the wall's width by 2. — A bubble level is a small tube of liquid with an air bubble inside. Air is less dense than the liquid, so the liquid pushes the bubble up to the highest spot. The tube bulges slightly in the middle, so when the level is perfectly flat, the highest spot is the center, and the bubble rests between the lines.
guides.teach: Let your child run the stud finder and mark each signal with painter's tape. Have them do the hook-height math on paper before anyone makes a hole. Make them the 'level reader' who calls out 'left side up' or 'right side up'.
mistakes: Hanging a heavy frame from drywall alone. — Use a stud, or an anchor rated for more than the frame weighs.
The screw suddenly goes in easily partway. — You've probably missed the stud. Find its center again, or switch to an anchor.
Measuring to the wire while it hangs loose. — Pull the wire up tight, the way it sits on the hook, before you measure.
Hanging a big mirror over the bed or couch. — Choose a spot where a fall couldn't land on anyone.
safety: Don't hang large pictures or mirrors over beds, couches, or chairs.
Use hardware rated for the weight. Check the package.
tips: Painter's tape lets you mark the wall without pencil smudges.
Check the anchor package for the weight it holds and the drill bit size it needs.
Skip patched or water-damaged drywall. Anchors can slip out of it.
Nails or hooks that go only into drywall or plaster are less secure than ones that reach a stud.

guides.name: Patch a Small Hole in Drywall
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 6, help from about 8, do it alone from about 11.
guides.intro: Nail holes, small dents, and dings show up in every home. For holes smaller than about 1/2 inch, a little spackle and a putty knife make them disappear. It's a good first repair, because a mistake can be sanded off and tried again.
need: Spackle (spackling compound)
Small putty knife
Fine sanding sponge or fine sandpaper
Damp cloth
Primer and matching paint
Small paintbrush

steps.how: This method is for small holes, under about 1/2 inch across. Bigger holes need a patch and joint compound.
Brush away loose bits and wipe off dust so the spackle sticks.
Scoop a little spackle onto the tip of the putty knife. Press it into the hole, then pull the knife across the wall to smooth it.
Spread the edges thin so they blend into the wall. After two or three strokes, stop and leave it alone.
Wait until it's completely dry. Small spots can dry quickly, but check the container for the time.
Sand gently with a fine sanding sponge until the patch is smooth and even with the wall.

steps.t: Add a second coat if needed
steps.how: Spackle shrinks a little as it dries, so a small dip may show. Add a thin second coat, let it dry, and sand again.
Prime the patch, then paint it to match. Without primer, the patch can look shinier or duller than the wall around it.

guides.how_it_works: What drywall is made of — Drywall is a sheet of gypsum pressed between two layers of heavy paper. Gypsum is a mineral, and most of the gypsum used in the United States goes into wallboard for homes and other buildings. — Chemically, gypsum is calcium sulfate dihydrate, written CaSO4·2H2O. 'Dihydrate' means two water molecules are locked into each unit of the crystal. That built-in water is about 20 percent of gypsum's weight, and it's part of why drywall resists fire: it takes a lot of heat to drive that water out. — Spackle from a tub is a paste with water in it. As the water evaporates, the paste dries, hardens, and shrinks a little. That's why a deep fill can sink and need a second thin coat.
guides.teach: Let your child fill old nail holes. Sanding fixes almost any mistake. Teach 'less is more': thin coats and just a few strokes. After painting, compare a primed patch with an unprimed one so they can see why primer matters.
mistakes: Sanding before the spackle is completely dry. — Wait the full drying time on the container.
Piling on one thick blob. — Use thin layers and let each one dry before the next.
Skipping primer. — Prime the patch so the paint's shine matches the rest of the wall.
Using spackle alone on a big hole. — Holes larger than about 1/2 inch need a patch and joint compound.
safety: If your home was built before 1978, its paint may contain lead. Sanding or scraping lead paint makes dust that is harmful, especially to children, so learn the lead-safe steps from EPA before you sand old paint.
tips: Fill the hole just slightly proud of the wall, since spackle shrinks as it dries.
Thin coats dry faster and sand more easily than one thick coat.
Prime and paint a whole section of wall if you want the color and shine to match evenly.
Keep leftover wall paint labeled with the room name for future touch-ups.

guides.name: Check Your Engine Oil
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 8, help from about 10, do it alone from about 13 with an adult nearby the first few times.
guides.intro: Engine oil keeps the moving metal parts inside your engine from grinding against each other. Checking it takes a few minutes and a clean rag. Too little oil can cause major engine damage, so this is a good habit to learn early.
need: Your car's owner's manual
A clean rag or paper towel
The motor oil your car needs, if you have to add some (look on the oil fill cap or in the owner's manual)
A funnel
before: Park on level ground so the reading is accurate.
Turn the engine off. Checking with a cold engine keeps your hands away from hot parts.
Keep your hands off the radiator hose and other engine parts, which can be hot after driving.

steps.how: Park on level ground and turn off the engine. Check before you start the car, or wait 5 to 10 minutes after shutting it off so the oil can drain back down.
Open the hood and prop it the way your owner's manual shows. The manual also shows where the oil dipstick is.
Pull the dipstick all the way out. Wipe the end clean with a clean rag.
Push the dipstick all the way back in. Then pull it straight out again.
Look at where the oil film stops. It should be between the lower and upper marks.

If the oil is at or below the lower mark, add the oil your manual lists through the oil fill cap, a little at a time. On most cars, about one quart raises the level from the lower mark to the upper mark.
Give the oil a couple of minutes to settle, then wipe and dip again. Stop at the upper mark. Too much oil can be as harmful as too little.
Push the dipstick fully back in, tighten the oil fill cap, and close the hood.

guides.pro: If you have to add oil often, have a repair shop check the car. If the red oil pressure warning light comes on, see the dashboard warning lights guide and have the car checked.
guides.how_it_works: Why engines need a slippery film — When two surfaces rub, friction pushes back against the motion. Inside an engine, metal parts slide and spin past each other the whole time it runs. Motor oil spreads a thin protective layer between them so they don't scrape and collide. It also helps keep the engine from overheating. — Viscosity means how much a liquid resists flowing. Honey has high viscosity. Water has low viscosity. Oil gets thicker when it's cold and thinner when it's hot. — A label like “5W-30” gives two ratings. The number before the W is the cold-weather rating: a lower number means the oil flows more easily when the engine is cold. The number after the dash tells how thick the oil is once the engine is warmed up. Thinner oil flows easily but makes a thinner protective film, so your engine is designed for one grade. Use the one on the oil fill cap or in your owner's manual.
guides.teach: Let your child pull and wipe the dipstick while you watch. Ask them to read the level out loud: below the low mark, between the marks, or at full. Show them where the oil grade is printed on the cap or in the manual. Pair the check with a regular errand, like getting gas, so it becomes a habit.
mistakes: Reading the dipstick on the first pull — Wipe it, push it all the way back in, and read the second pull.
Checking on a hill or slope — Park on level ground so the oil sits evenly in the engine.
Overfilling — Add a little at a time and recheck. Stop at the upper mark.
Using whatever oil is on the shelf — Use only the type your owner's manual lists.
safety: Check with the engine off.
Keep your hands away from hot engine parts like the radiator hose.
Wash your hands with soap and warm water after touching used oil.
tips: Look for the recommended oil grade on the oil fill cap. If it isn't there, check the owner's manual.
Wipe around the dipstick and oil cap before opening so dirt doesn't fall in.
Use a clean cloth on the dipstick. Grit on it can get into the engine.
Keep a quart of the right oil at home so you can top off when you need to.

guides.name: Check Tire Pressure and Tread
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 7, help from about 9, do it alone from about 12.
guides.intro: Tires are the only part of the car that touches the road. Keeping them at the right pressure and replacing them before the tread wears out helps the car grip, stop, and save fuel. All you need is a gauge and a penny.
need: A tire pressure gauge (keep one in the car)
A penny
Your car's tire pressure label or owner's manual
An air pump (many gas stations have one)
before: Check tires cold: the car should not have been driven for at least three hours.

steps.how: Look for the tire label on the edge of the driver's door or on the door post, or check the owner's manual. Use that number, not the one on the tire's sidewall. The sidewall number is the tire's maximum, not what your car needs.

steps.t: Make sure the tires are cold
steps.how: Check before you drive, or after the car has sat at least three hours. Warm tires read higher than cold ones.
Unscrew the valve cap, press the gauge firmly onto the valve stem, and read the psi. Write down each tire's number.
If a tire is low, add air and check again. If it's too high, press the pin in the valve stem with the edge of the gauge to let a little air out, then recheck. Screw the valve caps back on.
If your car has a spare tire, check it too.
Put a penny into a tread groove with Lincoln's head upside down and facing you. If you can see the top of his head, the tread is worn out and it's time for new tires.

steps.t: Look for wear bars and damage
steps.how: Raised bars run across the bottom of the tread grooves. If the tread is worn down level with them, replace the tires. Also look for cuts, cracks, or bulges.
Check all your tires at least once a month and before long trips.

guides.pro: Stop using a tire that has cuts, cracks, or bulges, and have a tire shop look at it. If the tire pressure light flashes for about a minute and then stays on, the monitoring system itself has a problem. Have a dealer or shop inspect it.
guides.how_it_works: Why cold mornings lower tire pressure — The air in a tire is made of tiny molecules zooming around. Every time they hit the inside of the tire, they push on it. All those pushes add up to the pressure your gauge reads. — When air warms up, the molecules move faster and hit the walls more, so pressure goes up. When air cools, they slow down and pressure drops. This is Gay-Lussac's law: if the space stays the same size, pressure rises and falls with temperature. — For car tires, AAA says pressure changes about 1 psi for every 10 °F change in temperature. So a 30-degree cold snap overnight can leave a tire about 3 psi low. That's why you check tires cold, before driving warms them up. — Low tires waste fuel, too. FuelEconomy.gov says gas mileage drops about 0.2% for every 1 psi drop in the average pressure of all four tires.
guides.teach: Let your child read the gauge and write the four numbers on a card. Make the penny test a game: is Lincoln's head hidden or showing? Have them find the door label and compare it with the sidewall so they see why the numbers differ. Measure on a cold morning and again after a drive, just to compare. Only adjust air when the tires are cold.
mistakes: Filling to the number on the tire's sidewall — Use the pressure on the door label or in the owner's manual. The sidewall shows the maximum.
Checking right after a drive — Warm tires read high. Check when the car has sat at least three hours.
Trusting your eyes — A low tire often looks normal. Use a gauge.
Forgetting the spare — Check it each month along with the others.
safety: Replace tires when the tread is worn down to 2/32 of an inch.
Don't drive on tires with cuts, cracks, or bulges.
Keep tires at the pressure your car's maker lists.
tips: The tire pressure warning light is a backup, not a replacement for monthly checks. It comes on only when a tire is well below the right pressure.
Tires can lose air suddenly after hitting a pothole or curb, so check them after a hard bump.
Front and rear tires may need different pressures. The label tells you.

Tires age even when the tread looks fine. Some carmakers and tire makers recommend replacing tires that are 6 to 10 years old. The last four digits of the DOT code on the sidewall show the week and year the tire was made.

guides.name: Change a Flat Tire
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 8, help from about 12 by handing tools and loosening lug nuts, and do it alone around the time they're learning to drive.
guides.intro: A flat tire can happen to anyone. If you're somewhere safe, you can put on the spare with the tools that came with your car. Practice once in your driveway so you're not learning on the side of the road.
need: Spare tire
The jack and lug wrench that came with your car
Owner's manual
Wheel wedges, if you have them
Tire pressure gauge
Gloves and a flashlight
before: Get to a safe spot, like a parking lot, side street, or wide shoulder, on solid, level ground away from traffic.
Turn on your hazard lights.
Put the car in Park, set the parking brake, and turn off the engine.
Get everyone out of the car and away from traffic. No one should stay inside a car that's being jacked up.
If changing the tire would put you or your passengers at risk, don't do it. Call roadside assistance instead.

steps.how: Put wheel wedges (or heavy objects) against the tire diagonally across from the flat so the car can't roll.
Take out the spare, jack, and lug wrench. Pry off the hubcap or wheel cover if there is one.
While the tire is still on the ground, turn each lug nut counterclockwise about a quarter to a half turn. Don't take them off yet.
Set the jack at the lifting point your owner's manual shows, on the car's metal frame near the flat. Plastic parts can crack if you jack on them.
Raise the car just until the flat tire is off the ground. Your manual may say how high. Never put any part of your body under the car while it's on the jack.
Remove the lug nuts by hand and put them where they won't roll away. Pull the tire straight toward you with both hands, smoothly, and lay it flat.
Line up the holes with the wheel studs and push the spare on. Make sure no mud or gravel keeps it from sitting flat against the hub. Thread the lug nuts on by hand.

steps.t: Lower and tighten in a star
steps.how: Lower the car until the spare touches the ground. Tighten the lug nuts with the wrench in a star (crisscross) pattern, not around the circle.

steps.t: Lower all the way and tighten again
steps.how: Lower the car fully, remove the jack, and go around the star pattern once more until every nut is tight.

steps.t: Check the spare and drive gently
steps.how: Check the spare's pressure; compact spares often need a higher pressure, such as 60 psi, so use the number on the spare's sidewall or in your manual. Stay within the spare's speed limit (often 50 mph) and get your regular tire fixed or replaced soon.

guides.pro: If you're on a busy highway or don't feel safe, stay away from traffic and call roadside assistance. Lug nuts need to be tightened to a set amount listed in your manual. If you don't have a torque wrench, have a tire shop check them as soon as possible. If a wheel stud or lug nut looks damaged, have a shop fix it. Damaged studs may not hold the wheel on.
guides.how_it_works: Levers, torque, and the jack — A lug wrench is a lever. Torque is the turning force you create, and it equals how hard you push times how far your hand is from the nut. Push with 50 pounds at the end of a 1-foot handle and you make 50 pound-feet of torque. Push the same 50 pounds on a 2-foot handle and you make 100 pound-feet. — That's why you push near the end of the handle. It's also why you loosen the nuts while the tire is still on the ground. If the wheel were in the air, it would just spin. On the ground, the tire's grip on the road holds it still, so your torque goes into the nut. — A car jack trades distance for force. You crank the handle around many times, moving your hand a long way, and the car rises only a little. If you ignore friction, the work you put in equals the work you get out, so a small push over a long distance can lift a heavy load a short distance. This is called mechanical advantage.
guides.teach: Practice in the driveway on a nice day, with an adult handling the jack. Let your child loosen and tighten lug nuts while the car is on the ground. Have them draw the star pattern for your car's number of lug nuts before you start. Find the jack points together, first in the manual and then on the car.
mistakes: Jacking up the car before loosening the lug nuts — Loosen them a quarter to half turn while the tire is on the ground.
Putting the jack under a plastic panel — Use the jack point shown in your manual, on the metal frame.
Tightening the nuts in a circle — Use a star pattern so the wheel sits evenly against the hub.
Driving fast or far on a compact spare — Follow the speed and distance limits on the spare or in your manual.
safety: Never put any part of your body under a car held up only by a jack.
Use only the jack that came with your car, at the jack points in the manual.
Block the wheel diagonally opposite the flat.
Keep everyone out of the car and away from traffic while you work.
tips: Check your spare's pressure when you check your other tires.
Lefty-loosey: turn lug nuts counterclockwise to loosen them.
Keep gloves and a flashlight with your spare.
A temporary spare isn't made to last. Get your regular tire fixed or replaced soon.
With practice, the whole job takes about 20 minutes.

guides.name: Jump-Start a Car
guides.time: about 15 minutes, plus a 20 to 30 minute drive
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 10, help from about 13 by reading the manual and naming each clamp spot, and do it alone around the time they start driving.
guides.intro: When a car's battery runs down, another car's battery can help it start. Jumper cables go on in a set order that keeps sparks away from the battery. Learn the order once and you can help yourself or a neighbor.
need: Heavy-duty jumper cables (AAA suggests a six-gauge, 16-foot set)
A working car with a 12-volt battery
Both cars' owner's manuals
Safety glasses
before: Read the jump-starting section of both owner's manuals. Some cars, including some hybrids and electric cars, have special rules or shouldn't be used to jump another car.
Check that both cars use 12-volt systems.
Look at the dead battery. Don't jump it if it's cracked, bulging, leaking, smells like rotten eggs, or is frozen.
Put on safety glasses and take off rings, watches, and other metal jewelry.
Park the cars close but not touching, both in Park with the parking brakes set and the engines off.

steps.how: Turn off the headlights, radio, and other electrical items in both cars.
Attach a red clamp to the positive (+) terminal of the dead battery.
Attach the other red clamp to the positive (+) terminal of the good battery.
Attach a black clamp to the negative (−) terminal of the good battery.

Attach the last black clamp to a solid, unpainted metal part of the dead car's engine, away from the battery, such as a thick bolt. Keep the cables clear of belts and fans, and never let the clamps touch each other.
Start the working car and let it run for three to five minutes.
Start the car with the dead battery. If it cranks slowly, wait about five more minutes and try again. If it won't start after a third try, the battery probably needs replacing.

Leave both cars running and connected for three to five minutes. Then remove the clamps in reverse order: black from the bare metal, black from the good battery, red from the good battery, and red from the car you just started.
Drive for 20 to 30 minutes so the car can recharge its battery. Have the battery tested soon, especially if it's more than three years old.

guides.pro: If the battery is cracked, bulging, leaking, or frozen, don't jump it. It needs to be replaced. If you're unsure about any step, get a trained technician or a tow service to help. If you hear a sharp, repeated clicking but the engine doesn't crank, the problem may be something other than the battery. Have a shop check it. If the battery keeps going dead or you don't know why it died, have the car checked.
guides.how_it_works: Why a weak battery can't crank the engine — A car battery is really six small batteries, called cells, connected in a row. Each lead-acid cell makes about 2 volts, so six of them add up to 12 volts. Inside, plates of lead and lead dioxide sit in sulfuric acid, and a chemical reaction pushes electrons through any circuit you connect. — Voltage is the push. Current is how much electricity flows. The starter motor that cranks the engine needs a very high current. In a circuit, current equals voltage divided by resistance. — Every battery also has some resistance inside it, and that inside resistance tends to rise as the battery runs down or ages. With a light load, a weak battery can seem fine. Under a heavy load like the starter, its voltage drops a lot, so the starter can't get enough current to turn the engine. — Jumper cables connect the good car's battery to the dead one so they share the work. Once the good car is running, its alternator helps charge the dead battery. After your car starts, its own charging system tops the battery back up while you drive.
guides.teach: Have your child read the jump-start page of the owner's manual out loud. Point out the + and − marks on the battery and the red and black cable colors. With the cables not attached to anything, have them say where each clamp goes, in order: red-dead, red-good, black-good, black-metal. Show them a good unpainted metal spot on your engine, away from the battery.
mistakes: Putting the last black clamp on the dead battery's negative terminal — Clamp it to bare metal on the engine, away from the battery, so any spark happens away from battery gases.
Letting the clamps touch each other — Hold the clamps apart and connect them one at a time.
Leaning over the battery while connecting — Stand to the side and keep your face back.
Jumping a damaged or frozen battery — Don't. Replace it.
safety: Batteries can give off hydrogen gas, which can explode. Keep sparks and flames away from the battery.
Wear safety glasses. Car batteries contain sulfuric acid, which is corrosive.
Use only a 12-volt source to jump a 12-volt car.
Keep hands, hair, and cables away from belts and fans once an engine is running.
tips: Keep jumper cables in your trunk.
Running the good car's engine a little above idle can speed up charging.
On the drive afterward, keep the air conditioner and rear defroster off so more power goes to recharging.
A short drive won't fix an old battery. Have it tested.

guides.name: Check Coolant, Brake Fluid, and Washer Fluid
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 8, help from about 10, do it alone from about 13.
guides.intro: Besides oil, your car needs a few other fluids: coolant so the engine doesn't overheat or freeze, brake fluid so the brakes work, and washer fluid so you can see. Most sit in see-through tanks with marks on the side, so a quick look tells you if one is low.
need: Owner's manual (it shows where each tank is and which fluids to use)
The exact coolant and brake fluid your manual lists, if you need to add any
Windshield washer fluid
A clean rag
A funnel
before: Park on level ground with the engine off and cold.
Never open the radiator cap when the engine is hot. Hot coolant and steam can spray out under pressure.
Keep coolant and washer fluid in their original containers with the caps closed tightly, out of sight and reach of children and pets.

steps.how: Open the hood and use your owner's manual to find the coolant reservoir, brake fluid reservoir, and washer fluid tank. The coolant reservoir is a see-through plastic tank, often near the radiator. The brake fluid reservoir usually sits toward the back of the engine area on the driver's side.
Look at the side of the coolant reservoir without opening it. The level should be between the low and full marks. On some tanks, the marks are labeled hot and cold.
If it's below the low mark, add the coolant your manual lists to the reservoir, up to the mark but not higher. Leave the radiator cap alone.
Wipe around the brake fluid cap so dirt can't fall in. The level should be between the MIN and MAX marks on the side of the reservoir.
Brake fluid drops a little as the brakes wear. If it's near or below the low mark, have a shop inspect the brakes soon. Use only the brake fluid your manual lists, and never mix types.
Open the washer fluid cap and fill the tank to the top. Where temperatures drop below freezing, use a winter washer fluid that resists freezing.
Wipe up any drips right away, tighten every cap, and close the hood.
If you find yourself adding coolant or brake fluid often, have a shop look for a leak.

guides.pro: If the brake fluid is near or below the low mark, have a shop inspect the brakes for wear or leaks as soon as possible. If you need to add coolant often, have the cooling system checked. If the engine is overheating or steaming, don't open the radiator cap. Let it cool and get help.
guides.how_it_works: How antifreeze works in winter and summer — Plain water freezes at 32 °F and boils at 212 °F, and both are a problem in an engine. Water that freezes in a cold engine can crack it. Water that boils turns to steam and stops cooling. — Coolant is a mix of water and antifreeze, which usually contains ethylene glycol. When something is dissolved in water, its particles make it harder for water molecules to line up into ice, so the mix freezes at a lower temperature. They also make it harder for water to escape as vapor, so the mix boils at a higher temperature. Chemists call these colligative properties: they depend on how many particles are dissolved, not on what kind they are. — More antifreeze gives more protection, up to a point. One Kia owner's manual says a half-and-half mix protects down to about −31 °F, and it warns against using more than 60% or less than 35% antifreeze. Your manual lists the right coolant for your car. — Brake fluid has its own chemistry problem. It slowly soaks up moisture from the air, and that lowers its boiling point. That's one reason to keep the cap closed and use fluid from a sealed bottle.
guides.teach: Have your child find each tank using the pictures in the owner's manual. Ask them to read each level out loud: below, between, or above the marks. Talk about why the radiator cap stays closed when the engine is hot. Do the salt-water freezer test together before your first winter check.
mistakes: Opening the radiator cap on a hot engine — Read the see-through reservoir instead, and only when the engine is cold.
Using the wrong coolant or brake fluid — Use only the type your manual lists, and don't mix types.
Using summer washer fluid in freezing weather — Switch to a winter washer fluid that resists freezing.
Storing fluids in drink bottles — Keep them in their original containers. People sometimes drink these fluids by mistake.
safety: Never open the radiator cap while the engine is hot.
Antifreeze and washer fluid are both poisonous. Antifreeze tastes sweet, which can attract children and animals.
Wipe up coolant spills and leaks right away.
Keep caps tightly closed and store bottles out of sight and reach.
tips: One Kia manual says to check coolant and its freeze protection at least once a year, at the start of winter, and before a trip somewhere colder. Check what your manual says.
Clean around caps before you open them so dirt doesn't get in.
Don't let brake fluid touch the car's paint. It can damage it.
Don't overfill. Too much fluid can be as harmful as too little.

guides.name: Replace Windshield Wiper Blades
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 7, help from about 9, do it alone from about 12.
guides.intro: Wiper blades are strips of rubber that clear rain and snow so you can see. Sun, weather, and use wear the rubber out, and then it streaks or skips. New blades usually click on in a few minutes.
need: New wiper blades in the right size
A towel
A tape measure
before: Turn the car off. Some cars need the wipers moved to a “service position” first; your owner's manual explains how.
Lay a towel on the windshield in case the wiper arm snaps back.

steps.how: Check your owner's manual or measure each old blade before you shop.
Lay a folded towel on the windshield under the wiper arm.
Gently lift the wiper arm up and away from the windshield.
Find the tab, button, or clip where the blade meets the arm. Press or lift it, then slide the blade down and off the hook.
Slide the new blade onto the hook until it clicks. Close any clip or latch.
Pull gently on the blade to make sure it's firmly attached.
Set the arm back down slowly. Don't let it snap onto the glass; that can crack or chip the windshield.
Replace the other blade the same way. If you used the service position, turn the car on to bring the wipers back. Spray washer fluid to test them instead of running them on dry glass.

guides.pro: If new blades still skip or don't touch the glass evenly, the wiper frame or arm may be bent. Have a shop check it.
guides.how_it_works: Why old wipers streak — A wiper works like a squeegee. Its rubber edge presses against the glass and pushes water off as it slides. The friction between rubber and glass depends on how hard they press together and on the two surfaces. — New rubber has a sharp, square edge that bends to fit the curve of the windshield. Over time, the sun's ultraviolet rays, ozone, very hot and cold weather, and grit wear the rubber down. The edge gets rounded, and the rubber dries out, hardens, and cracks. — A rounded or cracked edge can't press evenly on the glass, so water slips past and leaves streaks. Also, the grip needed to start something sliding is usually a bit bigger than the grip while it slides. A stiff blade that isn't gliding smoothly may stick and then jump, which you see as skipping or hear as chattering.
guides.teach: Let your child measure the old blades and write down the sizes. Have them hold the towel and lift the arm while you watch. Run a finger along an old blade and a new one to feel the difference in the edge. Talk about why seeing clearly in rain and snow matters for safe driving.
mistakes: Letting the bare wiper arm snap onto the windshield — Keep a towel on the glass and lower the arm gently.
Buying the wrong size — Check the manual or measure each old blade before you shop.
Running wipers on dry or icy glass — Spray washer fluid first, and clear ice with a scraper or the defroster.
Not clicking the blade all the way in — Tug gently to make sure it's locked before you lower the arm.
safety: Lower the wiper arm gently. If it snaps back, it can crack or chip the glass.
Replace blades once they streak or skip. Worn blades make it harder to see in rain, snow, and dust.
tips: Check your blades about every six months. Many mechanics and blade makers suggest replacing them every six months to a year.
Wipe the rubber edge with a damp paper towel to remove dirt and oil.
Clear ice with a scraper or the defroster, not the wipers.
Keep gasoline, paint thinner, and other solvents away from the blades.

guides.name: Read Dashboard Warning Lights
guides.teach_age: Learn the colors from about 8, quiz each other from about 10, and know the main lights well before driving lessons.
guides.intro: Warning lights are your car's way of telling you something needs attention. The color tells you how urgent it is, and the symbol tells you which system has a problem. Knowing the main ones helps you decide whether to keep going, pull over, or get help.
need: Your car's owner's manual (the warning light section)
A few minutes in the parked car

steps.how: Find the warning light section in your owner's manual. Symbols and meanings vary by car, so your manual is the final word.
Red means a problem that needs attention right away. Yellow or amber means something needs checking soon.
Turn the ignition to ON without starting the engine. Several warning lights glow, which shows they work. Lights like oil pressure and check engine should go out once the engine starts.

A steady light means the car's computer found a possible problem, often with emissions. Make sure the gas cap is tight; if the light stays on, have the car checked. If it flashes, the problem could cause serious damage, so avoid driving until it's repaired.
Oil pressure is low. Pull over as soon as it's safe, turn off the engine, and check the oil level. If the light stays on after adding oil, don't keep driving; have the car inspected.
The engine is overheating. Pull over when it's safe, turn off the engine, and let it cool before checking coolant or calling for help.
The charging system isn't working right; it could be the alternator or its belt, not only the battery. Get to a repair shop soon, before the battery runs down.
One or more tires are well below the right pressure. Check and fill them. If the light flashes for about a minute and then stays on, the monitoring system has a problem.

It comes on when the parking brake is set. If it stays on after you release the parking brake, the brake fluid may be low or the brakes may have a problem. Stop in a safe place; if you see a leak or the brakes don't feel right, don't drive. Have it towed.

guides.pro: A flashing check engine light: avoid driving until a technician repairs it. A brake light that stays on with the parking brake off, plus a leak or brakes that don't work right: don't drive; have the car towed. An oil pressure light that stays on after adding oil: have the car inspected before driving on. A charging system light: have the alternator and charging system checked soon.
guides.how_it_works: Sensors, the car's computer, and the tire light — Your car is full of sensors. A sensor measures something, like oil pressure, engine temperature, or how fast a wheel is turning, and turns it into an electrical signal. The car's computer keeps reading these signals. When a reading goes outside the safe range, the computer turns on a warning light. — The check engine light is part of the car's on-board diagnostics. When the computer finds a fault, it saves a trouble code, a short code made of letters and numbers that points to the problem. A mechanic plugs a scanner into the car to read it. — Tire pressure monitors work in one of two ways. Direct systems put a small battery-powered pressure sensor inside each tire that sends its reading to the car by radio. Indirect systems use the anti-lock brake sensors to compare how fast each wheel spins. A low tire is a little smaller around, so it has to spin faster to keep up. U.S. federal rules require the warning when a tire is 25% or more below the car maker's recommended pressure.
guides.teach: Make flash cards from the symbols in your manual: red ones in one pile, yellow ones in another. On the next drive, have your child watch the lights come on and go out during the bulb check. Play “what would you do?” with each red light. Show them where the warning light pages are in the manual.
mistakes: Ignoring a yellow light for months — Yellow means check soon. Look it up and get it looked at.
Driving on with a red oil pressure or temperature light — Pull over safely and turn off the engine. Driving on can badly damage the engine.
Guessing what a symbol means — Look it up in your owner's manual, since symbols vary by car.
Driving with the parking brake on — Make sure the brake light goes out before you drive.
safety: Treat red lights as urgent and pull over when it's safe.
Don't drive with the brake light on if the brakes feel wrong or fluid is leaking.
Avoid driving with a flashing check engine light.
Let an overheated engine cool before checking anything.
tips: A loose or broken gas cap can turn on the check engine light. Tighten it; if that was the problem, the light may go off after several trips.
The tire pressure light warns only when a tire is well below the right pressure, so keep checking tires monthly.
Notice whether a light is steady or flashing. That can change what it means.
Keep the owner's manual in the glove box.

guides.name: Change Your Own Oil and Filter
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 10, help from about 13 with jobs that keep them out from under the car, and do it alone as an older teen after doing it together a few times.
guides.intro: Over time, engine oil gets dirty and its additives get used up, so it needs to be drained and replaced. Changing it yourself teaches you how your car works, but only do it with the car safely supported on ramps or jack stands. If you're not comfortable, a shop can do it.
need: The oil type and amount your owner's manual lists
A new oil filter that fits your car
Car ramps or jack stands (never just the jack)
Wheel chocks
A wrench or socket for the drain plug
An oil filter wrench
A drain pan, funnel, rags, and newspaper
Safety glasses and gloves
A clean, leak-proof container with a tight lid for the used oil
before: Read the oil change section of your owner's manual.
Let the engine cool. Used oil and some metal parts can be very hot.
Park on flat, solid ground. Raise the car on ramps or jack stands as your manual shows, set the parking brake, and chock the wheels.
Never get under a car held up only by a jack.

steps.t: Set up under the drain plug
steps.how: Spread newspaper and set the drain pan under the drain plug. Open the oil fill cap on top of the engine so the oil drains faster.
Loosen the plug counterclockwise with the wrench, then finish by hand. Let the old oil drain for several minutes.
Check the plug and its gasket for wear, and use a new gasket if your manual calls for one. Put the plug back in and tighten it to the torque your manual lists.
Move the pan under the filter. Loosen it with the filter wrench, let it drain a few seconds, then remove it by hand. Make sure its rubber gasket came off with it and isn't stuck to the engine.
Rub a thin layer of oil on the new filter's rubber gasket. This helps keep it from cracking or sticking.
Screw it on by hand until it's tight. Tighten it by hand, not with the wrench, unless your manual or the filter's instructions say otherwise.
Using a funnel, pour in the amount and type your manual lists. Put the fill cap back on.
Start the engine and let it run for about two minutes. Look around the drain plug and filter for drips. If you see a leak, shut the engine off and find the cause before driving.
Bring the car back down to level ground, turn it off, and wait about two minutes. Check the dipstick and add a little more oil if needed.

Pour the used oil into your clean container and close it tightly. Take the oil and the drained filter to a used oil collection site, such as a service station, quick lube shop, or auto parts store that accepts them. Write down the date and mileage.

guides.pro: If you're unsure about any step, have a professional shop change the oil. Some carmakers recommend that. If a leak won't stop, have a shop look at it before you drive. If you don't have ramps or jack stands, don't go under the car. Have a shop do the job.
guides.how_it_works: Why oil wears out — Motor oil lubricates. It coats moving metal parts so they slide past each other with less friction. It also picks up dirt and the leftovers from burning fuel and carries them away from the pistons. — As you drive, more of that dirt builds up in the oil. The filter catches many of the particles, but over time the oil's additives get used up. Then the oil itself can start to break down: it reacts with oxygen (oxidizes) or thickens, and it can't protect the engine as well. — Used oil isn't garbage, though. It can be cleaned and re-refined into new motor oil that meets the same standards as oil made from crude. That's why recycling matters. Dumped oil pollutes water: California's recycling agency says one gallon of used oil can foul a million gallons of drinking water.
guides.teach: Before the first time, read the manual's oil section together and find the drain plug and filter on the car. Kids can hand tools, hold the funnel, pour new oil with help, and read the dipstick. Adults handle anything under the car. Have your child work out the next change mileage and write it down. Take the used oil to the recycling drop-off together.
mistakes: Working under a car held up only by the jack — Use ramps or jack stands on flat, solid ground every time.
Leaving the old filter gasket stuck on the engine — Check that it came off with the old filter before you put on the new one.
Overtightening the new filter with a wrench — Tighten it by hand unless the instructions say otherwise.
Pouring used oil on the ground, in the trash, or down a drain — Take it to a used oil collection site.
safety: Never get under a car supported only by a jack.
Wear safety glasses and gloves.
Let the engine cool first; used oil and metal parts can be very hot.
Set the parking brake and chock the wheels.
tips: Your owner's manual lists the oil change interval for your car. Intervals vary by maker and model year.
Don't mix used oil with anything else, including water.
Many service stations and quick lube shops take used oil and filters at no charge.
Drain the old filter before you take it to be recycled.

guides.name: Read a Paycheck
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 10, help from about 13, do it alone from about 15.
guides.intro: A pay stub shows what you earned, what was taken out, and what you actually take home. Reading one helps you catch mistakes, plan your spending, and see where tax money comes from. The rules here are U.S. federal rules; state rules vary.
need: A recent pay stub (or the sample numbers in this guide)
A calculator
Pencil and paper
Form W-4, when you start a new job

steps.how: Look for the dates the paycheck covers and the pay date. Your employer sets the pay schedule, such as every week or every two weeks.
Gross pay is everything you earned before anything is taken out. If you're paid by the hour, it's your hours times your hourly rate, plus any overtime.
This is federal income tax your employer holds back from each check and sends to the IRS for you. The amount depends on your pay and the Form W-4 you filled out.

Together these are called FICA. Social Security is 6.2% and Medicare is 1.45% of the wages they apply to. Multiply your gross pay by each rate and compare with your stub. Your employer pays a matching amount that doesn't come out of your pay.
Many stubs show state income tax withheld. Some states have no income tax, so this line may be missing. Rules differ from state to state.
These can include health insurance and retirement plan contributions. Some, like 401(k) contributions, are taken out before income tax withholding is figured, which lowers your taxable pay.

steps.t: Check that the math adds up
