steps.how: Add up every deduction and subtract the total from gross pay. The answer should match your net pay, the amount that actually lands in your account.
YTD shows totals from the start of the year through this paycheck. It tells you how much you've earned and paid in taxes so far this year.

steps.t: Fill out Form W-4 when you start a job
steps.how: Everyone fills in Step 1 (your information) and signs Step 5. Fill in Steps 2 to 4 only if they apply to you, such as a second job or dependents. The IRS Tax Withholding Estimator can help you choose.

steps.t: Update your W-4 after big changes
steps.how: Check your withholding early each year and after changes like a second job, marriage, or a new child. Too little withheld can mean a tax bill; too much means you wait for that money until your refund.

guides.how_it_works: Percentages on a pay stub — Social Security and Medicare are flat percentages of your pay. For 2026, Social Security is 6.2% of wages up to $184,500 for the year, and Medicare is 1.45% of all wages. An extra 0.9% Medicare tax is withheld on wages over $200,000 in a year. — To use a percent in math, change it to a decimal by dividing by 100: 6.2% becomes 0.062 and 1.45% becomes 0.0145. Then multiply by gross pay. — Worked example with made-up round numbers: gross pay is $1,000. Social Security is $1,000 × 0.062 = $62.00. Medicare is $1,000 × 0.0145 = $14.50. Say the stub also shows $60.00 of federal income tax and $30.00 of state tax. Total deductions are $62.00 + $14.50 + $60.00 + $30.00 = $166.50. Net pay is $1,000 − $166.50 = $833.50. — Federal income tax isn't one flat percent. It depends on your W-4, how often you're paid, and the tax brackets, so the example simply reads it off the stub.
guides.teach: Hand your child 10 play bills as 'gross pay,' then take some back for each tax line, so the gap between gross and net feels real. Let your child check the FICA math on one of your own pay stubs (cover anything private first). Before a first job, read Form W-4 together and talk through each step. Talk about what payroll taxes pay for: Social Security mainly funds retirement and disability benefits, and Medicare is a federal health insurance program.
mistakes: Planning to spend your gross pay — Plan with net pay. That's the amount you actually receive after taxes and deductions.

Claiming 'exempt' on Form W-4 when you don't qualify — For 2026 you can claim exempt only if you owed no federal income tax for 2025 and expect to owe none for 2026. To keep it for 2027, you must give your employer a new W-4 by February 16, 2027.
Not updating your W-4 after getting a second job — Two jobs can mean too little tax is withheld. Use Step 2 of the W-4 or the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator.
Never checking the numbers — Check the math each payday. Ask your employer about anything you don't understand.
tips: Use net pay, not gross pay, when you make a budget.
Ask your employer about direct deposit. If you can, split it so part of each check goes straight into savings.
Keep your Form W-2 at tax time. It sums up your pay and the taxes taken out for the year, and it's usually what you need to file.
Review the benefits your employer offers. Some can lower your taxable income.

guides.name: Make a Simple Budget
guides.time: about 1 hour to set up, then 10 minutes a week
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 8, help from about 10, do it alone from about 13.
guides.intro: A budget is a plan for your money: what comes in, what goes out, and what you save. It helps you notice when spending creeps up and makes room for goals and surprises.
need: Your take-home (net) pay and any other income
Receipts, a bank statement, or a banking app showing a month of spending
A notebook, spreadsheet, or the CFPB monthly budget worksheet
A calculator
A calendar for bill due dates

steps.how: Write down every source of money you get in a month. Use take-home pay, not gross pay, and include second jobs, allowances, or benefits.
Write down everything you spend, even small things. Receipts and your bank account make this easier. If a whole month feels like too much, start with one week.
Group your spending into categories like housing, utilities, groceries, transportation, phone, and eating out.
A need is something whose absence would put your health, safety, or ability to earn a living at risk. Most other things are wants. People's lists differ, and that's okay.

steps.t: Spot fixed, flexible, and occasional costs
steps.how: Fixed costs stay about the same, like rent or a phone plan. Flexible costs change, like groceries and entertainment. Occasional costs, like clothes or repairs, don't come every month.
Put each bill's due date on a calendar. If paydays and due dates don't line up, you can come up short even when the monthly totals look fine.
Decide how much to set aside for an emergency fund and your goals. Even a small amount helps. An automatic transfer from checking to savings makes it easier.
Subtract total spending and savings from total income. If the answer is positive, you have money left to save or spend. If it's negative, look at flexible spending first for cuts.
Each week or month, compare your plan with what you really spent. Update the budget when your job or spending habits change.

guides.pro: If debt is piling up, a reputable nonprofit credit counseling program may help. The FTC notes these may be offered through credit unions, universities, military personal financial managers, and Cooperative Extension offices.
guides.how_it_works: Percentages show where your money goes — A budget is mostly addition and subtraction: total income minus total spending tells you what's left. Percentages let you compare categories, even when your income changes from month to month. — To find what percent of your income goes to a category, divide the category total by your income and multiply by 100. — Worked example with made-up round numbers: take-home pay is $2,000 a month. Needs are rent $900, groceries $300, transportation $150, utilities $100, and phone $50, for a total of $1,500. Savings is $200. Wants are $300. Check: $1,500 + $200 + $300 = $2,000. — Needs are $1,500 ÷ $2,000 × 100 = 75%. Savings is $200 ÷ $2,000 × 100 = 10%. Wants are $300 ÷ $2,000 × 100 = 15%. The three percentages add up to 100%, which is a good way to check your work.
guides.teach: Give a small, regular allowance and let your child plan how to split it between spending and saving. Play a needs-or-wants sorting game with an old grocery receipt. Put a few real household bill due dates on a family calendar and talk about why timing matters. Track progress toward a savings goal on a chart and celebrate milestones along the way.
mistakes: Forgetting small purchases — Keep a daily log for a while. Small buys add up fast.
Leaving out bills that don't come every month — List yearly and occasional costs, divide each by 12, and set that amount aside every month.
Giving up after one bad month — Revise the plan using what you actually spent, and try again next month.
No line for savings — Treat savings like a bill. Set up an automatic transfer on payday if you can.
tips: Budget with net pay, not gross pay.
Plan for occasional costs, like birthdays, clothes, or car repairs, by setting aside a little each month.
Save windfalls, such as gifts or tax refunds, toward your emergency fund.
Keep your emergency fund somewhere safe and easy to reach, but not too tempting, such as a separate savings account.
Budgets are never perfect. The point is to notice when something costs more than you expected.

guides.name: Open and Use a Bank Account
guides.time: about 1 hour to open; 15 minutes a month to reconcile
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 8, help from about 11, do it alone from about 16.
guides.intro: A bank or credit union account keeps your money safer than cash at home and lets you get paid by direct deposit, pay bills, and use a debit card. Knowing your real balance at all times is the skill that keeps you clear of fees.
need: A photo ID and any other papers the bank or credit union asks for (check its website or call first)
Money for your first deposit
A check register, notebook, or spreadsheet
Your monthly statement (paper or online)

steps.t: Know the two main account types
steps.how: A checking account is for everyday spending, with a debit card, ATM access, and bill paying. A savings account is for setting money aside for goals and emergencies, and it may limit how often you can take money out.

steps.t: Choose an insured bank or credit union
steps.how: Check that a bank is FDIC-insured with the FDIC's BankFind tool; credit unions are insured by the NCUA. Standard FDIC coverage is $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each ownership category.
Before you open the account, ask about monthly fees, minimum balance fees, ATM fees, and what happens if you spend more than you have.

A bank can't charge an overdraft fee on one-time debit card purchases or ATM withdrawals unless you opt in. If you don't opt in, those purchases are usually declined instead. Checks and automatic payments can still bring fees.
Write down each deposit, debit card purchase, ATM withdrawal, check, automatic payment, and fee. Update your balance each time.
A debit purchase may take a day or two to post, so the balance in your app can differ from what you've really spent. Go by your own running balance.

When your statement comes, check off each item that matches your register. Add any fees or purchases you missed. Then adjust the statement balance for items that haven't cleared yet and compare the two.
If something is wrong or you don't recognize a charge, tell your bank right away, and no later than 60 days after the statement date. Follow up in writing and keep a copy.
If your card is lost or stolen, call your bank right away. Reporting within 2 business days generally limits what you can lose to $50 or less.

guides.pro: If your bank charged a debit card overdraft fee you never agreed to, you can file a complaint with the CFPB.
guides.how_it_works: Running balance and reconciling — Your balance changes with every transaction. Each new balance is the last balance plus money in, minus money out. Keeping this running total is how you avoid spending money you don't have. — Worked example: start with $250.00. Deposit a paycheck of $833.50: $1,083.50. Buy groceries with a debit card for $46.25: $1,037.25. Take $40.00 from an ATM: $997.25. Your $50.00 phone bill auto-pays: $947.25. — Reconciling: your statement shows an ending balance of $994.25 and a $3.00 ATM fee you didn't write down. Subtract the fee in your register: $947.25 − $3.00 = $944.25. The $50.00 phone payment hadn't cleared when the statement was made, so subtract it from the statement balance: $994.25 − $50.00 = $944.25. The two numbers match, so your account balances.
guides.teach: If your bank or credit union offers a youth savings account, open one together and let your child make the deposits. Show your child your banking app and point out pending versus posted transactions. Let a teen keep the register for one family account for a month, then reconcile it together.
mistakes: Going only by the balance in the app — The app may not show pending purchases or checks yet. Keep your own running balance.
Forgetting automatic payments — Write each recurring payment in your register or on a calendar before it happens.
Never reading the monthly statement — Reconcile every month so you catch fees, errors, and fraud early.
Waiting to report a lost card — Call your bank as soon as you notice. The sooner you report, the less you can lose.
safety: Report a lost or stolen debit card right away. Telling your bank within 2 business days generally limits your loss to $50 or less.
Check your account often. Reconciling regularly helps you spot fraud or identity theft.
Keep your money in an FDIC-insured bank or an NCUA-insured credit union.
tips: Turn on balance alerts on your phone if your bank or credit union offers them.
Write down ATM fees and other fees too; they're easy to miss.
Keep savings in a separate account so it doesn't mix with everyday spending.
Deposit insurance covers checking, savings, money market deposit accounts, and CDs. It does not cover stocks, bonds, mutual funds, crypto, or what's in a safe deposit box.

guides.name: How Interest Works
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 9, help from about 11, do it alone from about 14.
guides.intro: Interest is the price of using money. When you save, a bank pays you interest; when you borrow, you pay it. Compound interest can grow your savings over time, and it can also make credit card debt grow if you carry a balance.
need: A calculator with an exponent key (^ or x^y)
Paper and pencil
A savings account disclosure or a credit card statement, if you have one

steps.how: When you save, the bank pays you interest. When you borrow, you pay the lender. The starting amount is called the principal.
Simple interest is figured only on the principal. Compound interest is figured on the principal and on the interest already added, so it builds on itself.
Savings accounts show an annual percentage yield, or APY. It reflects the total interest paid over a year, including compounding, so use it to compare accounts.
Credit cards and loans show an annual percentage rate, or APR: the yearly cost of borrowing. It's the number to compare when you borrow.
Use A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt) to see what savings could grow to. The worked example below shows how.

steps.t: Use the Rule of 72 for a quick check
steps.how: Divide 72 by the yearly rate to estimate how many years it takes money to double. At 9%, that's about 8 years.
Credit card statements must show how long it would take, and how much it would cost in total, if you paid only the minimum each month.

steps.t: Pay the full balance when you can
steps.how: On most cards, you won't pay interest on purchases if you pay the full balance by the due date every month.

steps.t: If you carry a balance, pay more than the minimum
steps.how: Paying more each month cuts both the time it takes to pay off and the total interest you pay.

guides.pro: If card debt is hard to manage, look on your credit card statement: it lists a toll-free number for credit counseling information.
guides.how_it_works: The compound interest formula — In A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), P is the starting amount, r is the yearly rate as a decimal (5% = 0.05), n is how many times a year interest is added, t is the number of years, and A is the ending amount. — Worked example: you put $1,000 in savings at 5% a year, compounded monthly (n = 12), for 10 years. A = 1,000 × (1 + 0.05/12)^120 ≈ $1,647.01. With simple interest you'd have $1,000 + ($1,000 × 0.05 × 10) = $1,500. Compounding earned about $147 more. The APY for 5% compounded monthly is (1 + 0.05/12)^12 − 1 ≈ 5.12%. — Debt compounds too, working against you. Hypothetical card: a $1,000 balance at 24% APR (2% a month) and no new purchases. Paying $25 a month takes about 82 months, almost 7 years, and costs about $1,032 in interest. Paying $100 a month takes 12 months and costs about $127 in interest. Real cards usually use a daily rate, so actual numbers differ a little.
guides.teach: Pay a little 'family interest' on money your child leaves in a home savings jar for a month, so they see money earn money. Graph simple and compound growth side by side on graph paper and look for where the lines pull apart. Find the Minimum Payment Warning box on a real credit card statement together and read it out loud. The CFPB aims its lesson on minimum payments at ages 11 to 14, a good age to start this topic.
mistakes: Paying only the minimum on a credit card — Pay the full balance if you can, or as much over the minimum as you can.
Putting 5 instead of 0.05 into the formula — Change percents to decimals by dividing by 100.
Mixing up time units — Use the yearly rate for r, the number of times per year interest is added for n, and years for t.
tips: Compare savings accounts by APY and credit offers by APR.
Money left alone longer has more time to compound, so starting early matters.
An account's plain interest rate doesn't include compounding; its APY does.

guides.name: Credit Reports and Credit Scores
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 12, help from about 15, do it alone from about 18.
guides.intro: A credit report is a record of how you've handled credit, and a credit score is a number based on that record that predicts how likely you are to repay. Lenders use them when you apply for credit, so it pays to check your reports for free and fix mistakes.
need: Internet access or a phone
Your Social Security number (enter it only at AnnualCreditReport.com)
A pen or highlighter for marking errors
Copies of any papers that prove an error

steps.t: Go to the official free site
steps.how: Type AnnualCreditReport.com into your browser yourself. You can get free reports from Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion every week. You can also order by phone at 1-877-322-8228.
Each credit bureau may have different information, so check each one.
Make sure your name, addresses, and date of birth are right.
Look at each credit card and loan. Do you recognize it? Are payments shown as on time when you paid on time?
Look for late payments, collections, or bankruptcy. Accurate negative information can generally stay for 7 years, and bankruptcy for 10.

steps.t: Dispute errors with the credit bureau
steps.how: Explain in writing what's wrong and why. Include copies (not originals) of your proof and a copy of the report with the error circled. Use the bureau's online dispute or send it by certified mail with a return receipt, and keep copies.
Also write to the company that reported the wrong information, with the same details and copies of your proof.
The bureau generally has 30 days to investigate and must send you the results in writing. Check your report afterward to be sure the error is gone.
A freeze is free and stops anyone, including you, from opening new credit in your name. Place it with all three bureaus, and lift it for a lender when you need to apply.

guides.pro: If you find accounts you didn't open, that may be identity theft. An identity theft report from the FTC (or a police report) lets you place a free extended fraud alert that lasts 7 years.
guides.how_it_works: Why lenders care about your score — Lending money is a risk, because the lender might not get paid back. A credit score is a quick way to estimate that risk from your history. Many scores range from 300 to 850, but companies use different ranges, and you have more than one score. — According to the CFPB, scores look at things like how many accounts you have, how long you've had them, how close you are to your credit limits, and how often you've paid late. Paying your bills on time, every time, has the biggest effect. — One part you can calculate is credit utilization: the share of your available credit you're using. Experts cited by the CFPB suggest keeping it at no more than 30%. Example: a $300 balance on a card with a $1,000 limit is $300 ÷ $1,000 × 100 = 30%. — Applying for a lot of credit in a short time can hurt a score, because it can look like your money situation has gotten worse. Checking your own report doesn't count against you.
guides.teach: Pull your own free report and walk through each section with your teen (cover account numbers first). Parents can ask each bureau for a free credit freeze for a child under 16. It stays in place until you ask to remove it. Explain that a score is a prediction about paying back loans, not a grade on how good a person is.
mistakes: Using a look-alike website — Type AnnualCreditReport.com yourself. Many sites use 'free report' in their names or misspell the address.
Thinking that checking your report hurts your score — It doesn't. Checking your own report isn't an inquiry about new credit.
Checking only one bureau — Check all three; each can have different information.
Forgetting to lift a freeze before applying — Ask the bureau the lender uses to lift the freeze, then freeze it again afterward.
safety: Type AnnualCreditReport.com yourself. It and the credit bureaus won't email you asking for your Social Security number or account information.
A credit freeze is free. While it's in place, nobody can open a new credit account in your name, and it doesn't affect your credit score.
tips: Reports are free every week, so check them before you apply for credit.
A credit freeze doesn't affect your credit score.
If your report changes after a dispute, the bureau sends you a free updated copy.
If a dispute isn't settled your way, you can ask the bureau to add a statement about it to your file.

guides.name: File a Simple Federal Tax Return
guides.time: about 1 to 2 hours for a simple return
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 12, help from about 14, do it alone (with a parent checking) from about 16.
guides.intro: Each spring, U.S. workers file a federal tax return that settles up the income tax for the year before. If more tax was withheld from your paychecks than you owe, you get a refund; if less, you pay the difference. The figures here are for tax year 2026, the return you file in 2027.
need: Form W-2 from each employer
Any other tax forms you received, such as a Form 1099
Your Social Security number
A copy of last year's return, if you filed one
A free filing option (see the steps) or a paper Form 1040

steps.t: Check whether you need to file
steps.how: Use the IRS 'Do I need to file a tax return?' tool on IRS.gov. The answer depends on your income, filing status, age, and whether someone else can claim you as a dependent. Dependents have different rules, so teens should check.

steps.t: File even when you don't have to, if it helps
steps.how: If federal income tax was taken out of your pay, filing is how you get it back. You might also qualify for a refundable tax credit.
Collect a Form W-2 from every employer and any other tax forms you received. Keep last year's return handy if you filed one.

steps.t: Pick a free way to file
steps.how: IRS Free File offers free guided software from IRS partner companies; in the 2026 filing season it was for adjusted gross income of $89,000 or less, and each partner sets its own rules. Free File Fillable Forms are electronic IRS forms with little guidance. VITA sites offer free basic tax preparation in person. IRS Direct File was not offered in the 2026 filing season.
Your filing status affects your standard deduction and tax brackets. Most unmarried people without dependents file as Single.

On Form 1040, start with your income, then subtract the standard deduction. For tax year 2026 it's $16,100 for single filers. If someone can claim you as a dependent, yours is limited to the greater of $1,350 or your earned income plus $450.
Tax software, or the IRS tax table, applies the tax brackets to your taxable income. The example below shows how brackets work.

steps.t: Compare your tax with what was withheld
steps.how: If more was withheld than you owe, you get a refund. If less, you owe the difference.

Returns are generally due April 15, so April 15, 2027 for tax year 2026. If the date falls on a weekend or legal holiday, it moves to the next business day. Form 4868 gives you 6 more months to file, but not more time to pay.
Save a copy of your return and your W-2s in a safe place.

guides.pro: VITA (Volunteer Income Tax Assistance) offers free basic tax preparation for people who generally make $69,000 or less, people with disabilities, and taxpayers with limited English (2026 filing season figure). TCE (Tax Counseling for the Elderly) offers free tax help for people 60 and older. IRS Free File's guided software is free if your adjusted gross income is under that year's limit ($89,000 or less in the 2026 filing season).
guides.how_it_works: How tax brackets work — The U.S. uses marginal tax brackets. Your taxable income is split into layers, and each layer is taxed at its own rate. Moving into a higher bracket only changes the rate on the dollars above that line. — Tax year 2026 brackets for single filers (taxable income): 10% up to $12,400; 12% over $12,400 up to $50,400; 22% over $50,400 up to $105,700; 24% over $105,700 up to $201,775; 32% over $201,775 up to $256,225; 35% over $256,225 up to $640,600; 37% over $640,600. — Example: Jordan is single and earns $40,000 in wages in 2026. Taxable income is $40,000 − $16,100 = $23,900. Tax is 10% of the first $12,400 ($1,240) plus 12% of the next $11,500 ($1,380), for a total of $2,620. — Now Jordan gets a raise to $67,000. Taxable income is $50,900, which is $500 over the 22% line. Tax is $1,240 + 12% of $38,000 ($4,560) + 22% of $500 ($110) = $5,910. Only that last $500 is taxed at 22%; the dollars below the line are taxed just as before. (This example leaves out credits and other deductions.)
guides.teach: Look at a real W-2 and Form 1040 together and match the numbers from one to the other. Use the bucket activity to bust the myth that a raise can push all of your income into a higher bracket. Talk about why the government withholds tax from each paycheck instead of collecting it all in April.
mistakes: Thinking a higher bracket taxes all your income at the higher rate — Only the dollars above each bracket line get that bracket's rate.
Skipping a return when tax was withheld — Even if you're not required to file, filing may get your withheld tax back.
Assuming an extension gives you more time to pay — It doesn't. Pay what you owe by the original due date to limit interest and penalties.

Using the full standard deduction when a parent can claim you — Dependents use a different, often smaller standard deduction. The IRS tool and tax software handle this if you answer the dependent question correctly.
tips: Brackets and the standard deduction change every year for inflation. Use the figures for the tax year on your return.
If you can't file on time, file Form 4868 by the deadline and pay what you can. Interest builds on tax not paid by the original due date, and a late-payment penalty may apply.
You don't have to pay someone to file a simple return; free options exist.

guides.name: Spot and Avoid Scams
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 8, help from about 10, do it alone from about 13.
guides.intro: Scammers pretend to be people or groups you trust, then rush you into paying or sharing private information. Knowing the warning signs, and knowing that real government agencies never demand gift cards or crypto, protects you and your family.
need: Your phone, email, and social media accounts
A trusted adult or friend to talk to
ReportFraud.ftc.gov saved in your bookmarks

steps.how: Scammers pretend to be from a group you know, say there's a problem or a prize, pressure you to act right now, and tell you to pay in a specific way.
No government agency will demand that you wire money or pay with gift cards, cryptocurrency, or a payment app. The IRS generally contacts people by mail, and it won't threaten to have you arrested.

steps.t: Treat payment demands as a stop sign
steps.how: If someone says you can pay only by gift card, wire transfer, bank transfer, crypto, or a payment app, it's probably a scam.

steps.t: Don't trust caller ID or links
steps.how: Caller ID can be faked. Don't click links or open attachments in messages you didn't expect.

steps.t: Hang up and check for yourself
steps.how: Contact the company or agency using a phone number or website you look up yourself. For the IRS, check your online account or call 800-829-1040.

steps.t: Slow down and talk to someone
steps.how: Honest businesses give you time to decide. Anyone who tells you to keep it secret is a red flag. Talk to someone you trust before you act.
Don't give your Social Security number, passwords, or account numbers to anyone who contacted you out of the blue.
Contact the company you used to pay (your bank, card company, gift card company, or wire service) right away. Report the fraud and ask if the payment can be stopped or reversed.
Go to IdentityTheft.gov for steps based on what was exposed.
Tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Forward scam texts to 7726 (SPAM) and phishing emails to reportphishing@apwg.org.

guides.pro: Report scams to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and to your state attorney general. Report IRS impersonation scams to TIGTA (tigta.gov) and Social Security scams to the SSA Office of the Inspector General (oig.ssa.gov). If you shared personal information, IdentityTheft.gov has steps based on what was exposed.
guides.how_it_works: Why scammers rush you and want hard-to-trace money — A scam only works if you pay before you think it through. That's why scammers invent a problem or a prize and then push you to act now, sometimes telling you not to hang up or to keep it secret. Time works against the scammer, so taking your time is a strong defense. — Scammers also pick how you pay. Gift cards, wire transfers, bank transfers, crypto, and payment apps make it hard to get money back once it's sent. A credit card, by contrast, comes with more protections and ways to dispute a charge. — The stakes are real. The FTC says people reported more than $4 billion in losses last year to scams paid with bank transfers and cryptocurrency alone.
guides.teach: Practice saying 'I'll call you back' and hanging up. Make it a family habit. Agree on a family rule: no one buys gift cards or sends money because of a call, text, or message without talking to a parent first. Look at real scam texts on your phone together and point out the four signs. Talk about scams with grandparents and friends too; everyone can be a target.
mistakes: Calling back the number in the message — Look up the real number yourself on the official website or your statement.
Trusting caller ID — Caller ID can be faked. Hang up and call a number you know is real.
Depositing a check from a stranger and sending part of it back — Never do this. It's a common scam.
Waiting because you feel embarrassed — Act right away. Fast action can sometimes stop or reverse a payment.
safety: No government agency will demand payment by gift card, wire transfer, cryptocurrency, or payment app.
Don't click links or open attachments in messages you didn't expect.
Don't give personal or financial information in response to a request you didn't expect.
Social Security will never threaten, scare, or pressure you to act right away, and will never ask you to keep things secret.
tips: Block unwanted calls and filter unwanted texts on your phone.
Turn on multi-factor authentication so a stolen password isn't enough to get into your accounts.
Set your security software and phone updates to install automatically.
Before you pay someone new, search their name with words like 'scam' or 'complaint.'
When you can, pay with a credit card; it has more protections.

guides.name: Insurance Basics
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 12, help from about 15, do it alone from about 18.
guides.intro: Insurance is a deal: you pay a regular price, and the insurance company agrees to pay for certain big losses. Knowing the key words, especially premium, deductible, copay, and limit, helps you compare policies by what they really cost in a year.
need: Your state insurance department's website
Written quotes from several insurers
A calculator
A list of what you want covered

steps.how: The premium is what you pay for coverage. The deductible is the part of a loss you pay before the policy pays. A copay is a set dollar amount you pay for a medical service, such as $15 for a doctor visit. The limit is the most the policy will pay.

steps.t: Find out what your state requires
steps.how: Most states require some kind of car insurance to drive legally, but the rules vary. Your state insurance department can tell you what's required and whether your state uses a fault (tort) or no-fault system.

Liability pays for injuries and damage you cause to others. Collision pays for damage to your car from a crash. Comprehensive covers things like theft, hail, fire, and hitting an animal. Uninsured motorist coverage helps when the at-fault driver has no insurance.
State minimum liability amounts can be too low to cover you if you cause a serious crash. Higher limits often don't raise the premium much.

steps.t: Choose a deductible you could pay
steps.how: A higher deductible usually means a lower premium. Pick one you could afford to pay after a loss.
Get quotes from several insurers using the same coverages, limits, and information, and get them in writing.
Add the premium to what you'd likely pay out of pocket. A lower premium can mean higher costs when you actually need to use the insurance.
Ask about savings for things like insuring more than one car, bundling home and auto, safety devices, or a defensive driving course.

steps.t: Check the company and review each year
steps.how: Make sure the company and agent are licensed through your state insurance department. Review your options each year instead of renewing automatically.

guides.pro: Your state insurance department can tell you your state's insurance requirements and whether an agent or company is licensed.
guides.how_it_works: Comparing deductibles by total yearly cost — Insurance spreads risk. Many people pay premiums, and that money pays for the few who have big losses in a given year. That's why a premium reflects the losses the insurer expects. — Choosing a deductible is a trade-off: a higher deductible lowers your premium, but you pay more when you have a claim. You can compare plans by figuring the total you'd pay in a year. — Worked example with made-up numbers for car collision coverage: Plan A has a $500 deductible and a $1,200 yearly premium. Plan B has a $1,000 deductible and a $950 yearly premium. With no claims, A costs $1,200 and B costs $950. With one $3,000 claim, A costs $1,200 + $500 = $1,700 and B costs $950 + $1,000 = $1,950. With two such claims, A costs $2,200 and B costs $2,950. — Plan B saves $250 a year in premium but costs $500 more for each claim. So B comes out ahead in a year with no claims, and A comes out ahead in any year with at least one claim. Which is better depends on how likely a claim is and whether you could pay the higher deductible.
guides.teach: Look at your own health insurance card together and find the copays. Let a teen sit in when you shop for car insurance and fill in a comparison table of the quotes. Use the dice game to show that a higher deductible is a bet you might win or lose.
mistakes: Picking the lowest premium without looking at the deductible — Compare the total yearly cost, including what you'd pay if you had a claim.
Choosing a deductible you couldn't actually pay — Pick a deductible you could cover from savings after a loss.
Buying only the state minimum without thinking it over — Minimum limits may be too low for a serious crash. Price out higher limits too.
Comparing quotes with different coverages — Use the same coverages, limits, and information for every quote.
tips: If you have a car loan or lease, the lender may require collision coverage.
Ask each insurer how accidents and credit history could affect your rate.
Your driving record, the car you drive, where you live, and how much you drive can all affect the price of car insurance.
Short-term health plans often have lower premiums but cover less of your costs.

guides.name: Use a Food Thermometer and Cook to Safe Temperatures
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 6, help read the thermometer with an adult from about 8, and check food alone from about 12.
guides.intro: A food thermometer tells you when meat, poultry, egg dishes and leftovers are hot enough inside to be safe. You can't tell by looking. This guide gives the USDA safe minimum temperatures and shows you where to put the thermometer.
need: Food thermometer (a digital instant-read type is easiest to read)
Hot, soapy water to clean the thermometer
The safe temperature chart from FoodSafety.gov (the numbers are in step 1)
Oven mitts
before: Wash the thermometer stem in hot, soapy water before and after each use.
Read your thermometer's instructions so you know how deep to push it in. USDA says a digital instant-read thermometer needs to go in at least ½ inch, and a dial instant-read about 2 to 2½ inches.

steps.how: All poultry: 165 °F. Ground beef, pork, veal and lamb: 160 °F. Whole steaks, roasts and chops of beef, pork, veal and lamb: 145 °F, then a 3-minute rest. Fish: 145 °F. Egg dishes: 160 °F. Leftovers and casseroles: 165 °F.

steps.t: Check near the end of cooking
steps.how: Start checking a little before you expect the food to be done. USDA says it's safest to take the food off the heat before you take its temperature.
Push the tip into the thickest part of the food. Keep it from touching bone, fat or gristle.

steps.t: Go in from the side for thin foods
steps.how: For burgers and other thin foods, slide the thermometer in from the side until the tip reaches the center.

steps.t: Check whole birds in three places
steps.how: For a whole chicken or turkey, check the innermost part of the thigh, the innermost part of the wing, and the thickest part of the breast. Every spot needs to reach 165 °F.

steps.t: Check mixed dishes in several spots
steps.how: For casseroles and egg dishes, check the center or thickest part, then a few other spots.
If any spot reads below the target, put the food back on the heat and check again later.
After steaks, chops and roasts reach 145 °F, let them sit 3 minutes before you cut or eat them. During the rest, the temperature holds steady or keeps rising, which finishes killing germs.
Wash the stem in hot, soapy water before you use it again.

guides.how_it_works: Why the inside temperature matters, and why color can fool you — Raw meat, poultry and eggs can carry harmful bacteria. Heat kills them, but only when the food gets hot enough all the way through. The outside of a chicken breast heats first and the center heats last. That's why you measure the thickest part. — Time matters too. After a steak or roast comes off the heat, its temperature stays the same or keeps rising for a few minutes, and that extra heat destroys bacteria. Because of this, USDA says whole cuts of pork cooked to 145 °F with a 3-minute rest are as safe as the old advice of 160 °F with no rest. — Color is a poor guide. Ground beef can turn brown inside before it's hot enough to kill bacteria. USDA reports that about 1 in 4 hamburgers turns brown in the middle before it reaches a safe temperature. A thermometer measures what matters: the temperature inside.
guides.teach: Let your child read the number out loud while you hold the food steady. Before the thermometer goes in, ask them to point to the thickest part. Cut one cooked burger open together and talk about why you still check the temperature instead of trusting the color. Give them the job of washing the thermometer after every use.
mistakes: Judging doneness by color. — Use the thermometer every time. Ground beef can look brown before it's safe.
The tip is touching bone. — Pull back a little and move the tip into the meat, away from bone, fat and gristle.
Checking only one spot in a whole bird or a casserole. — Check the thigh, wing and breast of a bird, or several spots in a casserole.
Using the thermometer on raw food, then cooked food, without washing it. — Wash the stem in hot, soapy water between uses.
Cutting into a roast the moment it comes out. — Let whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb and veal rest 3 minutes after they reach 145 °F.
safety: Use a food thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes and leftovers. Color and texture aren't reliable signs of safety.
Take food off the heat before you take its temperature.
Wash the thermometer in hot, soapy water before and after each use.
tips: Fish is done at 145 °F, or when the flesh is opaque and flakes easily with a fork.
Shrimp, lobster, crab and scallops are done when the flesh is pearly or white and opaque. Clams, oysters and mussels are done when the shells open.
Raw ham needs 145 °F and a 3-minute rest. Reheat precooked ham to 165 °F, or to 140 °F if it was packaged in a USDA-inspected plant.
Keep the thermometer in the same drawer every time so it's easy to grab.

guides.name: Store Leftovers Safely
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 5, help pack leftovers from about 7, and put food away alone from about 10.
guides.intro: Leftovers save money and time, but they need to get cold fast. Bacteria multiply quickly in food left at room temperature. These steps follow USDA advice for cooling, storing and reheating leftovers.
need: Shallow containers with lids
Tape or labels and a marker
Appliance thermometer for the fridge and freezer
Food thermometer for reheating
before: Use an appliance thermometer to check that your fridge is at 40 °F or below and your freezer is at 0 °F or below.

steps.how: Get leftovers into the fridge within 2 hours after cooking. If it's hotter than 90 °F, like at a summer picnic, the limit is 1 hour.
Divide large amounts into shallow containers so the food cools quickly.
You don't have to wait for food to cool on the counter. Hot food can go straight into the fridge, or you can chill it first in a bowl of ice or cold water.
Write what it is and the date on the lid so you know when to use it.

steps.t: Eat or freeze within 3 to 4 days
steps.how: Leftovers keep 3 to 4 days in the fridge. If you won't eat them by then, freeze them.
Frozen food stays safe, but leftovers taste best if you eat them within 3 to 4 months.
Thaw frozen leftovers in the fridge, in cold water in a leak-proof bag, or in the microwave. Never thaw on the counter. You can also reheat straight from frozen; it just takes longer.
Heat leftovers until a food thermometer reads 165 °F. Bring sauces, soups and gravy to a rolling boil.
Cover the food and stir or turn it while it heats. Let it stand for a bit, then check the temperature in several places.

steps.t: Toss food left out too long
steps.how: Throw away perishable food that sat out more than 2 hours (1 hour above 90 °F). Reheating won't fix it, because some bacteria make toxins that cooking doesn't destroy.

guides.how_it_works: The danger zone and doubling bacteria — Bacteria grow fastest between 40 °F and 140 °F. Food safety experts call this the danger zone. In that range, the number of bacteria can double in as little as 20 minutes. — Doubling adds up fast. Start with 10 bacteria. After 20 minutes there could be 20, then 40, then 80. Two hours holds six 20-minute doublings, so 10 could become 10 × 2⁶ = 640. That's why the 2-hour rule exists. — Cold slows bacteria down, and freezing makes them go dormant, like they're asleep. Freezing doesn't kill them. When food thaws, they wake up and can multiply again. Some bacteria also make toxins that heat can't destroy, so reheating can't rescue food that sat out too long. — Shallow containers help because heat escapes through the food's surface. A thin, wide layer has lots of surface for its size, so its middle cools fast. A deep pot keeps its center warm for a long time.
guides.teach: Set a 2-hour timer when food comes off the stove and put your child in charge of it. Let them pick the containers and write the labels. Show them the fridge thermometer and have them check it once a week.
mistakes: Leaving a big pot of soup on the stove to cool overnight. — Split it into shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours.
Reheating only until it's warm. — Heat to 165 °F and check in several spots.
Thawing leftovers on the counter. — Thaw in the fridge, in cold water in a sealed bag, or in the microwave.
Keeping leftovers for a week or more. — Eat them within 3 to 4 days, or freeze them.
Not knowing how cold the fridge is. — Keep an appliance thermometer inside and make sure it reads 40 °F or below.
safety: Refrigerate perishable food within 2 hours, or within 1 hour if it's above 90 °F.
Keep the fridge at 40 °F or below and the freezer at 0 °F or below.
Reheat leftovers to 165 °F. Bring sauces, soups and gravy to a rolling boil.
tips: Small portions cool faster and are easier to reheat.
Cooked rice that sits out too long is a common cause of one type of food poisoning, so get it into a shallow container and into the fridge quickly.
Takeout and restaurant leftovers follow the same 2-hour rule.
Freezing keeps food safe, but it doesn't kill germs. Treat thawed food like fresh perishable food.

guides.name: Basic Knife Skills
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 6, cut with an adult right beside you from about 8, and use a chef's knife alone from about 12.
guides.intro: A sharp knife and a few good habits make cutting faster and safer. This guide covers how to hold the knife, how to hold the food, and how to wash and put knives away.
need: Chef's knife (8 to 10 inches), which handles most cutting jobs
Paring knife (3 to 4 inches) for small jobs
Cutting board
Damp kitchen towel, or a board with rubber feet
Practice foods like a zucchini, cucumber or potato
before: Put a damp towel under the cutting board, or use a board with rubber feet, so it can't slide.
Always cut on a cutting board. Never cut food while holding it in your hand.

steps.how: Set the board on a damp kitchen towel so it stays put while you cut.
Hold the handle close to the blade. This gives you better control.
With your other hand, hold the food with your fingertips curled under, like a claw. Tuck your thumb and little finger behind your other fingers, so your knuckles face the blade.
Round foods roll. Cut a potato or onion in half first, then set it flat side down before you keep cutting.

steps.t: Keep the tip on the board
steps.how: Cut with a rocking or see-saw motion, pushing slightly forward and away from your body. Keep the tip of the knife touching the board.
Let the sharp edge do the work. Smooth strokes beat hard pressing.
If a knife slips off the counter, step back and let it drop. Never try to catch it.
Carry a knife with the blade pointed down. Hand it over handle first, or set it down so the other person can pick it up.
Wash knives by hand after each use and dry them. Never leave a knife in a sink of soapy water, where someone could reach in and get cut.
Store knives in a knife block, on a magnetic strip, or with a blade guard. If you pause while cutting, lay the knife at the top of the board with the blade facing away from you.

guides.how_it_works: Why a sharp knife cuts with less force — Pressure is how much force pushes on each bit of area. The formula is pressure = force ÷ area. Push with the same force on a smaller area, and the pressure goes up. — A sharp knife's edge is very thin, so it touches the food along a tiny area. A small push makes a big pressure, and the food splits apart. A dull edge is wider and rounder. The same push spreads out, so the knife squashes or slides instead of cutting. — Here's an example with made-up numbers. A 5-pound push on an edge touching 0.01 square inch makes 5 ÷ 0.01 = 500 pounds per square inch (psi). The same push on a duller edge touching 0.1 square inch makes only 50 psi. — That's why a sharp knife is safer. A dull knife needs more force, and extra force makes it easier for the blade to slip off the food.
guides.teach: Practice the claw with no knife at all. Curl your fingers on a zucchini and 'walk' them back. Start with a steady food, like a zucchini cut in half and set flat side down, and stay right beside your child. Teach 'step back, don't catch' before the very first lesson. Have them say the habit out loud: 'Board steady, claw hand, tip down.'
mistakes: Cutting food while holding it in the air. — Always set the food on the cutting board first.
Fingers flat on top of the food. — Curl them into a claw with your thumb tucked behind.
The board slides around. — Put a damp towel or a rubber-footed board underneath.
Round food rolls away. — Cut a flat side first and set it down on that side.
Pressing hard with a dull knife. — Sharpen it. A sharp knife needs less force and is less likely to slip.
safety: Use a cutting board, never your hand.
Never try to catch a falling knife.
Never leave a knife in a sink of soapy water.
Carry knives blade down and pass them handle first.
tips: A serrated knife works well for bread and soft produce.
Keep knives sharp with a sharpening steel or a pull-through sharpener. Don't try to sharpen serrated knives at home.
Hold a few knives in your hand before you buy one, and pick the handle that feels comfortable.
Keep knives out of the dishwasher. Wash and dry them by hand.

guides.name: Cook Three Staples: Rice, Eggs and Pasta
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 6, help at the stove from about 9, and cook these alone from about 12.
guides.intro: Rice, eggs and pasta are cheap, filling and the start of many meals. Learn these three and you can always make dinner. Each one also shows a bit of kitchen chemistry.
need: 2- to 3-quart saucepan with a tight-fitting lid (rice)
Large pot that holds more than 4 quarts of water (pasta)
Colander
Frying pan, bowl, fork and spatula (eggs)
Measuring cups
Oven mitts
before: Wash your hands before you start.
Read the package directions for your rice and pasta. Different kinds need different amounts of water and time.

steps.how: Put 1 cup of long-grain white rice and 1¾ to 2 cups of water in a 2- to 3-quart saucepan.
Bring it to a boil, stirring once or twice. Turn the heat down low, cover with a tight lid, and simmer 15 minutes. Brown rice needs 2 to 2½ cups of water and 45 to 50 minutes.
If the rice isn't tender or there's still water, cover and cook 2 to 4 minutes more. Take it off the heat, fluff it with a fork, cover, and let it stand 5 minutes.
Use about 4 quarts of water for each pound of pasta. Keep the lid on so it boils sooner.
Add the pasta to the boiling water and stir. Stir again once it starts cooking so the pieces don't stick together.
Cook for the time on the package. Taste a piece; it should be a little chewy. Pour it into a colander in the sink, keeping your face away from the steam.
Crack the eggs into a bowl and beat them with a fork until blended.
Heat a frying pan with a little butter or oil over medium heat. Pour in the eggs and stir gently as they set. Keep cooking until no runny egg is left; scrambled eggs should not be runny.
Wash anything raw egg touched with hot, soapy water. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Hard-cooked eggs keep up to 1 week in the fridge.

guides.how_it_works: Starch soaks up water, and egg proteins unfold and set — Rice and pasta are mostly starch, packed into tiny grains called granules. When starch is heated in water, the granules soak up water and swell. Food scientists call this gelatinization. It's why hard rice turns soft, and why 1 cup of dry rice makes about 3 cups cooked. — Gelatinization only goes one way. Once the granules have swelled, cooked rice can't turn back into hard, raw grains. — Eggs change in a different way. Egg white is full of proteins. Each protein is a long chain folded into a special shape. Heat breaks the weak bonds holding that shape, so the proteins unfold. This is called denaturing. The unfolded proteins take up more room and tangle together, so a clear, runny egg white turns white and firm. — Cooking eggs until both white and yolk are firm also matters for safety. USDA notes that even clean, uncracked eggs can carry Salmonella bacteria.
guides.teach: Let your child measure the rice and water. It's good practice with fractions. Have them set a kitchen timer for each step. Stand beside them the first few times they drain pasta, and show how to pour away from their face. Have them crack eggs into a small bowl first, so any bits of shell are easy to scoop out.
mistakes: Lifting the lid again and again while rice cooks. — Keep it covered for the full time, then check.
Pasta clumps together. — Use about 4 quarts of water per pound, and stir right after adding it and again once it starts cooking.
Runny scrambled eggs. — Keep cooking until no liquid egg is left and they're firm.
Leaving the pot of rice on the stove all afternoon. — Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours in a shallow container.
safety: Cook eggs until both the white and yolk are firm.
Cook casseroles and other egg dishes to 160 °F.
Wash utensils and counters that touched raw egg with hot, soapy water.
Drain pasta carefully and keep your face away from the steam.
tips: Keep the lid on while rice simmers so the steam stays in.
Instant rice and flavored rice mixes have their own directions; follow the package.
Cook egg casseroles and quiche to 160 °F, checked with a food thermometer.
Don't wash eggs before storing them. Keep them in their carton in the fridge, not in the door.

guides.name: Do a Load of Laundry
guides.time: about 15 minutes of hands-on work, plus machine time
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 5, help sort and load from about 7, and do a load alone from about 10.
guides.intro: Clean clothes start with the care label. Then you sort, pick a water temperature, measure detergent and let the machines work. One small habit, cleaning the dryer's lint filter, also lowers the risk of a dryer fire.
need: Laundry detergent
The detergent's measuring cap or a measuring cup
Washer and dryer, or a drying rack
Your machines' owner's manuals
before: Make sure the lint filter is in the dryer. Never run a dryer without it.
Check that the washer and dryer are plugged directly into wall outlets.

steps.how: U.S. clothing labels must tell you how to wash and dry the item and warn you about steps that would harm it. If a label lists a water temperature, don't go hotter. Follow any 'Do not bleach' or 'Dry flat' instructions.
Keep whites away from colors. Wash very dirty clothes apart from lightly dirty ones, lint-shedding items apart from others, and delicate items apart from sturdy ones.
Some colored clothes bleed dye. If an item's color runs, wash it alone or with clothes of the same color.
Rub a little liquid detergent into collars, cuffs and other heavily soiled spots before washing.

Follow the label first. Hot water cleans heavy dirt and kills more germs, but it can fade some colors. Warm water handles lightly soiled clothes and is safe for most colors. Cold water suits some delicate fabrics; use a detergent made for cold water.
Use the amount on the detergent package for your load size and how dirty it is. Too much makes extra suds that keep clothes from getting clean. Too little leaves dirt and body oil behind.
Don't stuff the washer. Clothes need room to move so water and detergent can flow through them. If your washer has a water-level setting, match it to the load.
Before and after every dryer load, pull out the lint filter and clear off the lint.
Tumble dry, hang or lay flat, whichever the label says. Check for stains before anything goes in the dryer; see the stain guide.

guides.pro: Have your dryer installed and serviced by a professional, as the U.S. Fire Administration recommends. If the outdoor vent flap doesn't open while the dryer runs, or the vent behind the dryer is crushed or blocked, get it fixed before you use the dryer again.
guides.how_it_works: How detergent pulls grease off clothes — Water alone can't wash away grease, because oil and water don't mix. Detergent fixes that. Its molecules have two ends. One end is attracted to water (hydrophilic, 'water-loving'). The other end is attracted to oil (hydrophobic, 'water-fearing'). — In the wash, the oil-loving ends grab onto grease and body oil. The detergent molecules gather into tiny balls called micelles, with the oil trapped inside and the water-loving ends facing out. Now the water can carry the oil away when the washer drains and rinses. — Detergent also holds loosened dirt in the wash water so it doesn't settle back onto your clothes. That only works if the water can move, which is one reason not to overload the washer.
guides.teach: Make sorting a game with three piles: whites, darks, and 'ask me.' Read care labels together and match them to the machine settings. Make cleaning the lint filter your child's job every single time. Let them measure detergent with the cap and find the fill line.
mistakes: Washing a new red shirt with whites. — Keep whites apart, and wash new colors alone or with similar colors.
Adding extra detergent 'to be safe.' — Measure what the package says. Too many suds keep clothes from getting clean.
Stuffing the washer full. — Leave room for clothes to move.
Skipping the lint filter. — Clean it before and after every load.
Ignoring the care label. — Check it first, especially for 'Dry flat', 'Do not bleach' and temperature limits.
safety: Clean the lint filter before and after each dryer cycle.
Never run the dryer without the lint filter.
Plug washers and dryers directly into wall outlets.
Clean the dryer vent ductwork every year.
tips: Mix small items with large ones, like washcloths with sheets, so everything moves freely.
Care labels may use symbols instead of words. In the U.S., the FTC allows the ASTM symbol system.
A label that says 'Only non-chlorine bleach, when needed' means chlorine bleach would harm the item.
Check clothes as they come out of the dryer. If you see a spot, rub in a little detergent and wash again.

guides.name: Remove Common Stains
guides.time: about 15 minutes, plus soaking and washing
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 6, help blot and rinse from about 8, and treat everyday stains alone from about 12. Handle anything with bleach together with an adult.
guides.intro: Most stains come out if you act quickly and use the right method. The trick is knowing what kind of stain you have. This guide covers the basic rules and a few common stains.
need: Clean white cloths or paper towels for blotting
Liquid laundry detergent
Enzyme pretreatment or presoak product
A bowl or sink of cold water
Rubber gloves if you use bleach
before: Read the care label and the stain remover's label before you start.
Test any stain remover on a hidden spot, like a hem or seam allowance, to make sure it doesn't change the color.
When you use bleach or other strong products, open windows or work in a spot with plenty of fresh air.

steps.how: Treat stains as soon as you can. Fresh stains come out much more easily than old ones.
Press a clean cloth on a wet spill to soak it up. Rubbing can spread the stain and damage the fibers. Work from the back of the fabric to push the stain out.
Protein stains include blood, egg and grass. Oily stains include grease and cooking oil. Some, like chocolate, are both.

Soak blood, egg or grass stains in cold water; hot water can set them. For dried stains, scrape off what you can, then soak in cold water with detergent or an enzyme presoak. Don't use enzyme presoaks on silk or wool.
Rub full-strength liquid laundry detergent into the grease. Then wash in the hottest water the care label allows.
If some color remains, an all-fabric (oxygen) bleach is the gentler choice. Use chlorine bleach only if the fabric can take it, and never on silk, wool or spandex.
Rinse out the stain remover, then wash the item following its care label.
Look closely before anything goes in the dryer. Dryer heat can make a stain permanent. If it's still there, treat it and wash again, or let it air dry.

guides.pro: For 'Dryclean only' clothes, take the stain to a dry cleaner. Home dry-cleaning solvents can be highly toxic.
guides.how_it_works: Three ways to break up a stain — Stain removers work in three main ways. Enzymes are proteins that break big molecules into small pieces. Enzyme pretreatments break down protein stains like blood and grass so water can wash them away. — Detergents and solvents go after oily stains. Oil doesn't mix with water, so you need something that grabs onto oil, like the detergent molecules in the laundry guide. — Bleach is an oxidizer. Color comes from parts of molecules called chromophores. Bleach breaks chemical bonds in those parts, so the molecule stops absorbing visible light and the color disappears. That's why bleach can lift a stain, and also why it can fade your shirt. — Heat matters too. Hot water can set protein stains, a bit like the way heat sets an egg white. That's why blood goes in cold water.
guides.teach: Keep a small stain kit (cloths, liquid detergent, enzyme pretreatment) where kids can reach it. Teach the short rule: blot, cold water, check before drying. Store bleach and other cleaners up high and out of sight of young children, and use bleach together until your child is older.
mistakes: Scrubbing hard at a fresh spill. — Blot gently, working from the back of the fabric.
Rinsing blood in hot water. — Use cold water. Heat sets protein stains.
Drying a shirt before the stain is gone. — Check first. Treat and rewash if needed.
Using chlorine bleach on wool, silk or spandex. — Check the label and use only what it allows.
Mixing cleaners to make them 'stronger.' — Never mix bleach with ammonia, acids like vinegar, or any other cleaner.
safety: Never mix bleach with ammonia or any other cleaner. Bleach plus ammonia makes chloramine gas. Bleach plus acids, including vinegar and some toilet bowl cleaners, makes chlorine gas.
Read and follow the safety instructions on every product you use.
Wear gloves and keep fresh air flowing when you use bleach.
Store bleach up, away and out of sight of children.
tips: If you can't tell what a stain is, skip hot water.
For chocolate, rub in liquid detergent first for the oily part, then treat any color that's left.
Rinse stain remover out before washing so it can't react with other products.
Never iron a stained spot. Heat sets stains.

guides.name: Rent Your First Place
guides.time: a few weeks of planning before you move
guides.teach_age: Talk through a rent budget together from about 12, compare real listings from about 15, and sign a lease yourself once you're an adult.
guides.intro: Renting your first apartment is a big money step and a legal one. A lease is a contract, so you need to know what you're signing. This guide covers budgeting, spotting scams, reading the lease, deposits, renters insurance and the move-in check. Tenant laws are different in each state, so always check your own state's rules.
need: Your monthly income and a simple budget
Money for move-in costs, such as the first month's rent and a security deposit
A phone camera
A notebook or move-in checklist
A folder for your lease, receipts and photos
before: Look up your state's tenant rights before you sign anything. USA.gov points to state housing agencies, attorneys general and state tenant handbooks.

steps.how: HUD counts a household as 'cost burdened' when housing costs, including utilities, are more than 30% of its monthly income. Aim to keep rent plus utilities at or under that line.
Ask which utilities you'll pay, such as electricity, gas, water, trash and internet. Get the answer in writing.

See the place in person if you can. Search the address along with the owner's or company's name to check for copied listings. Walk away if someone rushes you or wants payment by wire transfer, gift card or cryptocurrency.
Read every line before you sign, and ask about anything you don't understand. Don't count on promises that aren't written in the lease. Keep a signed copy.

A security deposit is money the landlord holds in case of unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear. State law sets the limits. In Massachusetts, for example, the deposit can't be more than the first month's rent.

Your landlord's insurance covers the building, not your belongings. Renters insurance can pay to repair or replace your things if they're damaged or stolen, and its liability part helps if you're blamed for someone's injury or property damage.

On move-in day, walk through every room. Write down every problem and take photos. If your state uses a move-in 'statement of condition' form, fill it out. This keeps you from being blamed for damage you didn't cause.
Pay rent on time and get a receipt every time you pay. Massachusetts, for example, gives tenants the right to a receipt for every payment.
Report problems to your landlord in writing; email counts. Keep copies of what you send and what you get back.
If you have a dispute, reread your lease first. Then contact your state's tenant rights agency, your attorney general's office, or legal aid.

guides.pro: If you can't settle a problem with your landlord, look for free or low-cost legal aid, or contact your state attorney general or housing agency.
guides.how_it_works: The 30 percent line, and why a lease is a contract — Rent is usually the biggest bill a renter pays each month. HUD uses 30% of income as a common line. When housing costs, including utilities, take more than 30% of a household's monthly income, HUD calls that household cost burdened. Less money is left for food, transportation and savings. — You can turn the line into a quick check: multiply your monthly income by 0.30. With a made-up monthly income of $2,000, that's 0.30 × 2,000 = $600 for rent plus utilities. If a place costs more, you'd need more income, a roommate or a cheaper place. — Renting has a civics side too. A lease is a contract, a set of promises the law will enforce. Most rules about deposits, repairs and evictions come from state and local law, which is why they vary so much. For example, the Massachusetts Attorney General says a landlord there can never force a tenant to move out without going to court first.
guides.teach: Look at real rental listings together and add up the full monthly cost. Read a sample lease out loud and circle anything confusing. Practice a move-in walk-through in your own home: list every scuff and take photos. Talk about scams. What would make a deal seem too good to be true?
mistakes: Budgeting for rent but forgetting utilities. — Ask which utilities you pay and add them to the total.
Paying a deposit for a place you haven't checked out. — Visit if you can, search the address and owner, and never pay by wire, gift card or crypto.
Signing a lease you only skimmed. — Read every line and get any promises written in.
Skipping the move-in check. — List every problem and take photos on day one.
Assuming the landlord's insurance covers your stuff. — It doesn't. Get renters insurance.
safety: Never pay rent or a deposit by wire transfer, gift card or cryptocurrency. The FTC says anyone who insists on those is running a scam.
tips: Rent that's much cheaper than similar places nearby can be a sign of a scam.
Get every promise in writing. Email counts.
Keep your lease, receipts, photos and repair emails together in one folder.
Ask whether a renters policy pays replacement cost (new items) or actual cash value (what your used items were worth). Replacement cost costs more but pays more.

guides.name: Apply for a Job
guides.time: a few hours over a week or two
guides.teach_age: Practice a résumé and a mock interview from about 13, and apply for a first job from about 14 to 16, depending on federal and state rules.
guides.intro: A first job teaches skills you can't learn in class and gives you money you earned yourself. Getting hired takes a few pieces: a résumé, references, a careful application, a good interview and a thank-you note. If you're under 18, federal and state laws limit when and where you can work.
need: Your phone number and a professional email address
A list of your school, activities, and any work or volunteer experience with dates
Two to three references who've agreed to be contacted
Printed copies of your résumé
A work permit or age certificate, if your state requires one
before: If you're under 18, check your state labor department's rules. Federal law doesn't require work permits, but many states do for workers of certain ages.

steps.t: Check the rules for your age
steps.how: Under federal law, 16 is the basic minimum age for most jobs. At 14 and 15 you can work only certain non-hazardous jobs, outside school hours: no more than 3 hours on a school day and 18 hours in a school week. If state and federal rules differ, the stricter one applies.
Write down your contact details, your school, your activities, and any jobs or volunteer work with dates and contact names.

List your education, any work or volunteer experience, activities, awards and skills. Start each bullet with an action verb. Keep it to one page in 10- to 12-point type, and ask someone to proofread it.
Pick teachers, school leaders, past employers or other adults who know your work, not family or friends. Ask them first, and tell them they may get a call.

steps.t: Write a short cover letter if asked
steps.how: Say which job you want and why you're interested in that business. Then connect your skills to the most important things the job needs.
Answer every question, and write 'N/A' instead of leaving a blank. On paper, use black or blue ink, spell carefully, and sign and date it. Proofread before you turn it in.
Learn the basics about the business. Practice answers to common interview questions out loud, and write down a few questions to ask them.
Dress for the job, silence your phone and arrive 15 minutes early. Bring copies of your résumé, a separate list of two to three references, your questions, and a notebook and pen.
Within a day, send each interviewer a short thank-you note or email.
If you haven't heard back within a week, call the person who set up your interview.

guides.pro: If an employer asks you to work hours or do tasks that seem off-limits for your age, contact your state labor department or the U.S. Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division.
guides.how_it_works: Trading your time and skills for pay — A job is a trade. You give an employer your time and skills, and the employer pays you wages. Businesses hire when they have work that needs doing and believe you can do it well. — Employers can't see your skills just by looking at you. A résumé, references and an interview are how you show them. A careful application and a thank-you note are evidence that you're reliable, which is part of what they're paying for. — Your pay depends on your wage and your hours. Gross pay, your pay before anything is taken out, equals hourly wage × hours worked. If you're 14 or 15, federal law caps a school week at 18 hours and a non-school week at 40 hours, so those limits shape how much you can earn.
guides.teach: Hold a mock interview at the kitchen table, then trade roles. Help your child list everything they've done: babysitting, volunteering, clubs, sports, yard work for neighbors. Proofread the résumé together, out loud. Practice thank-you notes on something easy first, like a note to a relative for a gift.
mistakes: Listing references without asking them. — Ask first, and let them know a call may come.
Leaving blanks on the application. — Answer every question. Write 'N/A' if it doesn't apply.
Sending the same letter everywhere. — Name the job and the business, and match your skills to what they need.
Arriving right on time, or late. — Plan your route and arrive 15 minutes early.
Never following up. — Send a thank-you within a day, and call if you've heard nothing in a week.
tips: Use a simple, professional email address. Avoid nicknames.
Keep your voicemail greeting professional and check messages often while you're job hunting.
Make sure the dates and details on your résumé match your application.

For 14- and 15-year-olds, federal law allows work only between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m., except June 1 through Labor Day, when the evening limit is 9 p.m. Federal law doesn't limit hours for 16- and 17-year-olds in non-hazardous jobs, but many states do.

guides.name: Register to Vote and Get Ready to Vote
guides.time: about 15 minutes to register, plus time to learn your ballot
guides.teach_age: Talk about elections from about 8, read a sample ballot together from about 12, and register yourself when your state allows, which in most states can be before you turn 18.
guides.intro: Voting is how citizens choose the people who make laws and run government. Before you can vote, most states require you to register, and each state sets its own deadlines and rules. This guide walks through the steps. It doesn't tell you who or what to vote for.
need: Your state or local election office's website (vote.gov links to every state)
Your home address
An ID, if your state requires one to vote
A calendar for deadlines

steps.how: To vote, you must be a U.S. citizen, meet your state's residency rules, be 18 by Election Day, and be registered by your state's deadline. North Dakota doesn't require voter registration.
There's no national registration deadline. Some states close registration 30 days before Election Day, and others let you register on Election Day itself.

Most states let you register online. You can also mail in the National Mail Voter Registration Form (New Hampshire, North Dakota, Wisconsin and Wyoming don't accept it), or register in person at your election office or state motor vehicles office.
In most states you can sign up before you turn 18. Several states let 17-year-olds vote in primary elections if they'll be 18 by the general election.

Look yourself up on your state's election website. Make sure your name, address and polling place are right. Check before the registration deadline so there's time to fix problems, and update it if you've moved.
Many election offices post sample ballots online. Read about each race and any ballot questions. If you use a voter guide, check who wrote it.

Most people who vote on Election Day vote in person at an assigned location. Some states hold elections entirely by mail, and others let you request an absentee ballot. Ask your election office which options you have.
Voting hours and locations are set locally. Confirm your voting location and its hours with your election office before each election.
Check your state's ID rules. In most states you need ID to vote in person. You don't need a voter registration card.

guides.pro: If you have questions about whether you can vote or about your registration, contact your state or local election office.
guides.how_it_works: How your vote turns into representation — The United States is a representative democracy. Instead of voting on every law, citizens elect people to make laws for them. You vote for leaders at every level: local, state and federal. — In Congress, the House of Representatives has 435 members, and each serves a two-year term. The Senate has 100 senators, two from each state, and each serves a six-year term. — All 435 House seats are on the ballot every two years. Senate terms are staggered, so only about one-third of senators are elected in any two-year cycle. Midterm elections fall halfway between presidential elections.
guides.teach: Read a sample ballot together and look up what each office does. Practice finding your state's election office website. Teach the process, not the choices. Let kids form their own views as they grow. Mark registration deadlines and election dates on the family calendar.
mistakes: Missing the registration deadline. — Look up your state's deadline early. Some states close registration 30 days before Election Day.
Assuming you're still registered after a move. — Check your registration and update your address.
Going to the wrong voting location. — Confirm your location and hours with your election office before Election Day.
Seeing the ballot for the first time in the booth. — Read your sample ballot ahead of time.
Forgetting ID. — Check your state's ID rules before you go.
tips: Register early instead of waiting for deadline week.
Check your registration again after any move.
Mail ballots can go back by mail, to your local election office, or in an official drop box, which needs no stamp.
If your registration shows as 'inactive,' contact your election office early. You may need extra steps before you can vote.
